modules.title: Introduction to Trello: What It Is and Why Organize with It
modules.content:
### A Day‑to‑Day Moment That Changes Everything  

Imagine you’re juggling three different projects at once: planning a weekend getaway with friends, tracking your freelance invoices, and coordinating a small community garden. You’ve got sticky notes on the fridge, a spreadsheet on your laptop, and a mental checklist that never seems to shrink. By mid‑afternoon, you realize you’ve missed a deadline, forgotten a reservation, and can’t remember if the garden’s watering schedule is up to date.  

What if you could see all those moving parts in one place, slide tasks from “to‑do” to “done” with a single drag, and instantly share the view with anyone who needs to be in the loop? **That is the promise of Trello**, a visual productivity platform that turns scattered information into an organized, easy‑to‑navigate board.

---

## What Is Trello?  

**Trello** is a web‑based (and mobile) application that helps individuals and teams organize work, projects, and everyday life using a visual board system. At its core, Trello is a **digital Kanban board**—a method that originated on factory floors to visualize workflow and limit work‑in‑progress.  

The platform’s primary purpose is to **make work visible**, allowing you to:

* Capture ideas, tasks, and information in one place.  
* See the status of each item at a glance.  
* Move items through stages of completion with a simple drag‑and‑drop.  
* Collaborate in real time, so every participant shares the same up‑to‑date view.

Because it is visual, flexible, and intuitive, Trello works for everything from a single person’s grocery list to a multinational product launch.

---

## Core Components: Boards, Lists, and Cards  

Trello’s simplicity rests on three building blocks that you’ll use in every project.

### Boards: Your Project Canvases  

A **Board** is a dedicated workspace for a specific project, goal, or area of life. Think of it as a large whiteboard you can access from any device. Each board contains its own set of lists and cards, keeping unrelated projects completely separate.

* **One board per project** – e.g., “Vacation 2024,” “Freelance Invoicing,” or “Community Garden.”
* Boards can be **private**, **team‑visible**, or **public** (shareable via a link).  
* You can add a **cover image** or **background color** to make the board instantly recognizable.

### Lists: Stages or Categories  

Within a board, **Lists** are vertical columns that represent stages of a workflow, categories, or any logical grouping you choose. The classic Kanban setup uses “To Do,” “Doing,” and “Done,” but you can customize them however you like.

* Typical list uses include:
  * **Workflow stages** – Backlog → In Progress → Review → Completed.  
  * **Time‑based categories** – This Week, Next Week, Later.  
  * **Types of content** – Ideas, Research, Drafts, Published.  

Lists are flexible; you can reorder them, rename them, or add as many as you need.

### Cards: The Heart of Trello Tasks  

A **Card** lives inside a list and represents an individual item you want to track—usually a task, but it can also be an idea, a reference, or a piece of information.

* **What a card can hold**:
  * A **title** (the main description).  
  * **Checklists** for subtasks.  
  * **Due dates** and **reminders**.  
  * **Attachments** (files, images, links).  
  * **Comments** for discussion and notes.  
  * **Labels** (color‑coded tags) for quick visual grouping.  

You move cards from one list to another to reflect progress—dragging a “Book Flights” card from “To Do” to “Done” instantly shows that the task is complete.

---

## How Trello Differs from Traditional Tools  

Many people start with spreadsheets, plain text to‑do lists, or paper planners. Trello offers several distinct advantages that address the shortcomings of those tools.

### Spreadsheets: Structured Data vs. Visual Flow  

| Feature | Spreadsheet (e.g., Excel, Google Sheets) | Trello |
|---------|-------------------------------------------|--------|
| **Visualization** | Tabular rows/columns; requires manual formatting for visual flow. | Drag‑and‑drop board; visual status at a glance. |
| **Collaboration** | Real‑time editing possible, but change tracking can be messy. | Automatic live updates; each participant sees the same board instantly. |
| **Flexibility** | Adding new columns or rows can disrupt formulas; limited to grid layout. | Add or reorder lists without breaking anything; cards can hold any type of data. |
| **Learning Curve** | Requires understanding of cells, formulas, and sometimes scripting. | Intuitive interface; no formulas needed for basic use. |

Spreadsheets excel at heavy data analysis, but they are less suited for tracking the *state* of work items in a fluid, visual way.

### To‑Do Lists: Linear Simplicity vs. Multi‑Dimensional Organization  

| Feature | Classic To‑Do List (paper or app) | Trello |
|---------|-----------------------------------|--------|
| **Linear Order** | Tasks are ordered one after another; limited ability to group or prioritize visually. | Lists allow multiple parallel streams; cards can be reordered within a list. |
| **Collaboration** | Usually personal; sharing requires copying or external communication. | Built‑in sharing; teammates can add, comment, and move cards together. |
| **Context** | Minimal context—usually just a title. | Cards can hold rich context (attachments, checklists, comments). |
| **Scalability** | Becomes unwieldy with dozens of tasks. | Handles hundreds of cards across many lists while staying readable. |

To‑do lists are great for quick personal reminders, but they lack the structure needed for complex projects or team collaboration.

### The Core Advantages of Trello  

* **Visual Overview** – Instantly see what’s pending, in progress, and completed.  
* **Drag‑and‑Drop Simplicity** – No need to type commands or edit formulas; moving a card updates its status.  
* **Real‑Time Collaboration** – Everyone sees changes as they happen, reducing miscommunication.  
* **Customization** – Add labels, colors, checklists, and more to fit any workflow.  
* **Cross‑Platform Access** – Use on web browsers, desktop apps, or mobile devices; all sync automatically.

---

## Real‑World Use Cases  

Trello’s flexibility means it can serve many different needs. Below are three common categories with concrete examples.

### 1. Personal Organization  

* **Meal Planning & Grocery Shopping** – Create a board with lists for “Weekly Meals,” “Shopping List,” and “Prepared.” Add recipe cards, attach PDFs, and check off items as you shop.  
* **Habit Tracking** – Use a list for each habit (e.g., “Exercise,” “Read,” “Meditate”) and create daily cards that you move to “Done” each day.  
* **Travel Planning** – Lists for “Flights,” “Accommodation,” “Activities,” and “Packing.” Attach itineraries, add checklists for items to pack, and set due dates for payment deadlines.

### 2. Work & Professional Projects  

* **Freelance Client Pipeline** – Lists for “Leads,” “Proposals Sent,” “Contract Signed,” “In Progress,” and “Delivered.” Cards hold client briefs, contracts, and deliverable checklists.  
* **Sprint Planning (Agile Teams)** – A board with “Backlog,” “To Do,” “In Progress,” “Review,” and “Done.” Cards represent user stories; team members move them as work advances.  
* **Content Calendar** – Lists for each month or week; cards are blog posts or social media pieces, each with a due date, draft, and publishing checklist.

### 3. Team Projects  

* **Event Coordination** – Lists for “Planning,” “Vendors,” “Marketing,” “Day‑Of Schedule,” and “Post‑Event Debrief.” Team members assign themselves to cards, attach contracts, and comment on progress.  
* **Product Launch** – Separate boards for “Feature Development,” “Beta Testing,” and “Launch Marketing.” Cross‑board links keep everyone aligned.  
* **Non‑Profit Volunteer Management** – Lists for “Open Roles,” “Applicants,” “Onboarded,” and “Active Volunteers.” Cards store volunteer bios and shift schedules.

These scenarios illustrate how the same three components—boards, lists, cards—adapt to vastly different contexts while preserving a consistent user experience.

---

## Getting Started: Create a Free Trello Account  

A Trello account is required to save boards, collaborate, and sync across devices. The free tier provides unlimited personal boards, unlimited cards, and basic Power‑Ups (integrations) that are more than enough for beginners.

### Step‑by‑Step Sign‑Up  

1. **Visit the Trello website** – Go to **[trello.com](https://trello.com)**.  
2. **Click “Sign Up”** – The button appears prominently on the home page.  
3. **Enter your email address** – Use any valid email; you can also sign up with Google or Apple for a quicker process.  
4. **Create a password** – Choose a strong password (at least 8 characters, mixing letters, numbers, and symbols).  
5. **Verify your email** – Trello will send a confirmation link; click it to activate your account.  
6. **Complete the onboarding wizard** – Trello may ask what you intend to use it for (personal, work, team). Select the option that matches your primary goal; you can change this later.  

> **Tip:** If you’re part of a team at work or school, ask whether a **Team** (formerly “Organization”) account exists. Joining an existing team can give you immediate access to shared boards.

### Navigating the Dashboard  

Once logged in, you land on the **Dashboard** (also called the Home view). Here’s what you’ll see:

* **Top Navigation Bar** – Contains links to **Boards**, **Templates**, **Home**, **Notifications**, and **Profile**.  
* **Recent Boards** – Thumbnails of boards you’ve opened recently, for quick access.  
* **Starred Boards** – Boards you’ve marked with a star (favorite) appear in a dedicated section.  
* **Create New Board** – A bright “+” button in the upper‑right corner lets you start a new board instantly.  
* **Workspace Switcher** – If you belong to multiple workspaces (e.g., “Personal,” “Marketing Team”), a dropdown lets you toggle between them.  

Hovering over a board thumbnail reveals options to **Open**, **Star**, **Rename**, or **Delete**. Clicking a board opens its full view, displaying its lists and cards.

### First Look at a Sample Board  

To help you get comfortable, Trello offers a **“Welcome Board”** template that demonstrates the core features:

1. **Open the Welcome Board** – Click the “Explore Boards” link on the dashboard and select “Getting Started.”  
2. **Explore Lists** – Notice the three default lists: “To Do,” “Doing,” and “Done.”  
3. **Interact with Cards** – Drag the “Read the Trello Guide” card from “To Do” to “Doing.” Observe the subtle animation—this is the same action you’ll use for every task.  
4. **Add a Comment** – Click the card, type a quick note, and press **Enter**. Your comment appears instantly, visible to anyone else who opens the board.  

By playing with this sample board, you’ll see how easy it is to create, move, and enrich cards without any prior experience.

---

## Why Organize with Trello?  

Beyond its visual appeal, Trello delivers concrete productivity benefits:

* **Reduced Mental Load** – Externalizing tasks onto cards frees your brain to focus on the work itself.  
* **Clear Priorities** – Seeing all cards in one view helps you decide what to tackle next.  
* **Transparency for Teams** – Everyone knows who owns which task and its current status, cutting down on status‑update meetings.  
* **Scalable Simplicity** – Start with a single personal board; later, add more boards, invite collaborators, and enable Power‑Ups as your needs grow.  

These advantages translate into faster project completion, fewer missed deadlines, and a more satisfying sense of control over your workload.

---

## Key Takeaways  

* **Trello is a visual, web‑based productivity platform** that uses boards, lists, and cards to organize work and life.  
* **Boards** hold entire projects; **Lists** represent stages or categories; **Cards** are individual items that can contain rich details.  
* Compared with spreadsheets and traditional to‑do lists, Trello offers superior visual overview, real‑time collaboration, and flexible context for each task.  
* Common use cases span personal planning (meal prep, habit tracking), professional work (client pipelines, sprint boards), and team projects (event coordination, product launches).  
* Setting up a free account is quick: sign up with an email, verify, and explore the dashboard’s recent, starred, and template boards.  
* The dashboard provides easy navigation, and the built‑in “Welcome Board” lets beginners practice moving cards, adding comments, and using checklists.  

With these fundamentals in place, you’re ready to dive into creating your first board and shaping a workflow that truly works for you.

modules.title: Creating Your First Trello Board: A Step-by-Step Guide
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Moment: Planning Your Weekend Get‑Together

Imagine you’ve just been asked to organize a weekend hike for a group of friends. You need a place to capture ideas—trail options, gear checklists, a schedule, and a way to keep everyone in the loop. You could scribble on a napkin, send a long email chain, or—better yet—open a fresh Trello board. Within minutes you’ll have a visual, shareable plan that lives online, can be edited on the fly, and shows every task at a glance. Let’s walk through exactly how you create that board from scratch, give it a purpose‑clearing name and description, personalize its look, decide who can see it, and invite the right people to help.

---

## 1. Starting a New Board

### 1.1 Locate the “Create Board” Button  

1. **Log in** to your Trello account at trello.com (or open the desktop app).  
2. In the top‑right corner of the home screen you’ll see a **“+” (plus) icon**. Click it.  
3. From the dropdown, select **“Create Board…”**.  

> *If you’re on a mobile device, tap the **“+”** at the bottom of the screen, then choose “Create Board”.*

### 1.2 Choose a Starting Point  

You’ll be presented with two options:

| Option | When to use it |
|--------|----------------|
| **Start from scratch** | You have a brand‑new project (like the weekend hike). |
| **Use a template** | You want a pre‑built structure (e.g., a meeting agenda). |

For our scenario, click **“Start from scratch.”**

---

## 2. Naming and Describing Your Board

### 2.1 Give It a Clear Title  

A board’s title appears at the top of every view, so make it descriptive yet concise.  
**Example:** `Weekend Hike – June 10‑11, 2024`

- **Tip:** Include the date or a keyword that instantly tells you what the board is about. This helps when you have many boards over time.

### 2.2 Add a Board Description (Optional but Helpful)  

Below the title field, there’s a **“Add a description”** box. This is where you clarify the board’s purpose for anyone who might join later.

**Sample description:**  
> “Planning the group hike to Eagle Ridge. Includes trail research, gear checklist, transportation logistics, and post‑hike celebration ideas.”

- **Why it matters:** The description appears in the board’s **“About”** section, giving collaborators context without them having to read every card.

### 2.3 Save Your New Board  

After entering the title (and optional description), click **“Create Board.”** You’ll be taken to an empty board ready for customization.

---

## 3. Personalizing the Board’s Look

A visually appealing board makes it easier to locate and can boost motivation. Trello offers two main ways to change the background: **color** or **image**.

### 3.1 Changing the Background Color  

1. Click the **“Show Menu”** button on the far right of the board (three horizontal dots).  
2. Select **“Change Background.”**  
3. Choose from the palette of solid colors.  

- **Best practice:** Pick a color that reflects the theme of your project (e.g., a forest green for a hike).

### 3.2 Adding a Cover Image  

If you prefer a picture:

1. In the same **“Change Background”** menu, switch to the **“Photos”** tab.  
2. You can search Trello’s free library (e.g., type “mountains”) or click **“Upload Image”** to use a personal photo.  
3. Once selected, the image becomes the board’s backdrop.

- **Tip:** Use a high‑resolution image that isn’t too busy; otherwise, cards and text become hard to read.

### 3.3 Setting a Board Cover (Optional)  

For a more subtle visual cue, you can add a **cover image** to the board itself (the small square that appears in your home view). Click the board’s thumbnail in the home view, then **“Change Cover”** and repeat the steps above.

---

## 4. Understanding Board Visibility

Trello lets you decide who can see or edit your board. The three visibility levels are:

| Visibility | Who can see it? | Typical use case |
|------------|-----------------|------------------|
| **Private** | Only you (and any invited members) | Personal projects, confidential plans |
| **Team‑visible** | Everyone in a specific Trello team (e.g., “Family”) | Shared family calendars, work‑group initiatives |
| **Public** | Anyone on the internet (read‑only) | Open‑source documentation, community roadmaps |

### 4.1 Setting the Visibility  

1. Open the board menu (**“Show Menu”** > **“Settings”**).  
2. Click **“Change Visibility.”**  
3. Choose **Private**, **Team**, or **Public**.  

For the weekend hike we’ll keep it **Private**—only the invited friends should see the details.

### 4.2 When to Switch Visibility  

- **Private → Team:** If the project expands to a work group that already has a Trello team, switching makes onboarding easier.  
- **Team → Public:** When you want to share a roadmap publicly (e.g., an open‑source release plan).  

> **Remember:** Even a public board can be edited only by members you add later; the public setting merely grants **view‑only** access to anyone else.

---

## 5. Inviting Collaborators

A board becomes truly useful when others can contribute. Trello lets you add **members** (full collaborators) or **guests** (limited‑role users). For a weekend hike, you’ll likely invite each friend as a member.

### 5.1 Finding the Invite Option  

1. In the board menu, click **“Invite”** (often displayed as a person‑plus icon).  
2. A dialog appears with a field to enter email addresses or usernames.

### 5.2 Sending Invitations  

- **Enter each friend’s email** (or Trello username if they already have an account).  
- Optionally, add a **personal note**—e.g., “Hey, please add your gear items to the checklist!”  
- Click **“Send Invitation.”**  

Each invited person receives an email with a link to join the board. Once they accept, they appear under **“Members”** in the board menu.

### 5.3 Managing Member Permissions  

All members have the same default permissions: they can add, move, edit, and delete cards and lists. If you need finer control (e.g., some users should only view), you would need a **Business Class** or **Enterprise** subscription—outside the scope of this beginner module.

### 5.4 Removing or Changing Members  

If a friend can’t attend, you can remove them:

1. Open the board menu, click **“Members.”**  
2. Hover over the member’s avatar, click the **“X”** that appears, and confirm removal.

---

## 6. Quick Tour of the Newly Created Board

At this point your board contains:

- **A clear title and description** that explain its purpose.  
- **A customized background** (color or image) that matches the project theme.  
- **Private visibility** ensuring only invited friends can see it.  
- **Invited collaborators** ready to add their own cards and checklists.

You’re now set to start building **Lists** (the next module) and **Cards** (the following module). The board’s visual layout will instantly reflect any additions you make, keeping the entire planning process transparent for everyone involved.

---

## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

| Pitfall | Why it Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Forgetting to set a description** | New users think the title alone is enough. | Always add a brief description; it saves confusion later. |
| **Choosing a too‑busy background image** | Aesthetic appeal outweighs readability. | Prefer solid colors or simple images; test readability by adding a dummy card. |
| **Leaving the board public unintentionally** | Default may be “Team‑visible” if you belong to a team. | Double‑check visibility after creation, especially for personal projects. |
| **Inviting the wrong email address** | Typos or outdated contacts. | Verify email addresses before sending; Trello will flag invalid formats. |
| **Not notifying collaborators of the board’s purpose** | Members join silently and wonder what to do. | Use the personal note field in the invite dialog to give a quick “next steps” cue. |

---

## 8. Checklist: Board‑Creation Essentials  

- [ ] Click **“+” → Create Board** and select **Start from scratch**.  
- [ ] Enter a **descriptive title** (include date or project keyword).  
- [ ] Write a concise **board description** that clarifies the purpose.  
- [ ] Choose a **background color or image** that reflects the theme.  
- [ ] Set **visibility** to Private (or Team/Public as needed).  
- [ ] **Invite** all collaborators, adding a brief note if helpful.  
- [ ] Verify that members appear under **Board > Members**.  

Completing this checklist guarantees a functional, personalized board ready for the next steps in your Trello journey.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Creating a board** starts with the **“+”** button and the **“Create Board”** dialog.  
- **Naming** the board clearly and adding a **description** give instant context to anyone who opens it.  
- **Background customization** (color or image) is optional but improves visual cueing; keep readability in mind.  
- **Visibility settings** control who can see the board: **Private** (you + invited members), **Team‑visible**, or **Public** (read‑only).  
- **Inviting collaborators** is done via the **Invite** option; members can edit the board, while guests have limited access.  
- A quick **checklist** ensures you haven’t missed any essential step before moving on to lists and cards.

You now have a fully configured board—personalized, secure, and ready for collaboration. In the next module you’ll learn how to structure that board with **Lists** that represent workflow stages, turning your blank canvas into a living, organized plan. Happy planning!

modules.content:
## What a List Really Is  

When you open a Trello board you’re looking at a **digital Kanban board** – a visual playground where work moves from left to right. The vertical columns you see are **Lists**. Think of a list as a **container** that groups cards (your individual tasks) by a shared characteristic. In the classic “To Do → In Progress → Done” workflow, each of those words represents a separate list.  

A list does three things:  

* **Defines a stage** in your process (e.g., “Ideas” or “Awaiting Review”).  
* **Groups similar cards** so you can see at a glance what belongs together.  
* **Acts as a traffic‑light** – moving a card from one list to the next signals progress.

Because lists sit directly on a board, they inherit the board’s visibility settings (private, team‑visible, or public). This means anyone who can see the board also sees every list on it.

---

## Creating Your First List  

If you’ve already built a board (see Chapter 2), you’re ready to add your first list. Follow these steps:

1. **Locate the “Add a list” button** – it sits at the far right of any existing lists, or in the empty space if the board is brand‑new.  
2. **Click the button** – a small input field appears.  
3. **Type a name** – e.g., “Backlog”.  
4. **Press **Enter** or click **Add List**.  

Your new list appears as a vertical column. You can immediately start adding cards (covered later) or continue shaping the board.

> **Tip:** If you’re not sure about the exact name, you can always rename the list later (see the next section).

---

## Naming Lists to Match Your Project Stages  

The power of a list lies in its name. A clear, purposeful label tells anyone looking at the board what the cards inside represent. Below are common naming patterns, plus suggestions for customizing them to your own workflow.

### Classic Kanban Flow  

| List Order | Typical Name | What It Holds |
|------------|--------------|---------------|
| 1 | **To Do** | New tasks that haven’t been started. |
| 2 | **In Progress** | Tasks currently being worked on. |
| 3 | **Done** | Completed tasks, ready for review or archive. |

### Time‑Based Columns  

* **Today** – tasks you intend to finish today.  
* **This Week** – work slated for the current week.  
* **Next Week** – items you’ll tackle later.

### Content‑Type Separation  

* **Bugs** – defect reports.  
* **Features** – new functionality requests.  
* **Documentation** – write‑ups, guides, or help articles.

### Priority Buckets  

* **High‑Priority** – must‑do items.  
* **Medium‑Priority** – important but not urgent.  
* **Low‑Priority** – nice‑to‑have tasks.

### Hybrid Example  

Imagine you’re launching a small app. Your board could look like this:

1. **Ideas** – raw concepts, not yet vetted.  
2. **Backlog** – approved ideas waiting for a slot.  
3. **Sprint 1** – work planned for the first two‑week sprint.  
4. **Sprint 2** – next sprint’s tasks.  
5. **Done** – finished features ready for release.

#### Quick Checklist for Naming Lists  

- **Be concise** – a few words are easier to scan.  
- **Use verbs or nouns consistently** – e.g., “To Do” vs. “In Progress”.  
- **Reflect your team’s language** – if your team talks about “Stories”, use that term.  
- **Avoid jargon** unless everyone understands it – keep it inclusive for newcomers.

---

## Reordering Lists to Optimize Your Workflow  

A list’s position on the board is more than aesthetic; it shapes the mental flow of work. Here’s how to reorder them:

1. **Hover over the list header** – a six‑dot “handle” appears on the left side.  
2. **Click and hold** the handle.  
3. **Drag the list left or right** to the desired spot.  
4. **Release** – the board automatically saves the new order.

### Best‑Practice Ordering Strategies  

| Strategy | When It Works Best | Why |
|----------|-------------------|-----|
| **Left‑to‑Right chronological** | Projects with clear stages (e.g., To Do → In Progress → Done) | Mirrors natural reading direction, reducing cognitive load. |
| **Top‑to‑Bottom priority** | Boards where priority trumps stage (e.g., High → Medium → Low) | Highlights the most urgent work at the leftmost position. |
| **Grouped by type** | Teams handling multiple content types (e.g., Bugs, Features, Docs) | Keeps similar tasks together, easing navigation. |
| **Hybrid** | Complex workflows (e.g., “Backlog → Sprint 1 → Sprint 2 → Done”) | Combines stage progression with time‑boxing. |

#### Quick Reorder Exercise  

1. Create three lists: **Ideas**, **Backlog**, **Done**.  
2. Drag **Backlog** between **Ideas** and **Done**.  
3. Notice how the visual flow now moves from concept to execution to completion.

---

## Using Lists to Separate Different Types of Tasks or Categories  

Beyond stages, lists can serve as **category containers**. This is especially useful when a single board tracks multiple streams of work that don’t share a linear progression.

### Example: Marketing Campaign Board  

| List | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| **Content Creation** | Drafts, graphics, copy. |
| **Social Media** | Posts scheduled for each platform. |
| **Paid Advertising** | Ad copy, budgets, targeting. |
| **Metrics** | Reports, KPIs, performance dashboards. |

Each list holds cards that belong to that category, making it simple to locate the right piece of work without scrolling through unrelated items.

### Benefits of Category‑Based Lists  

- **Clarity** – teammates instantly know where to add a new task.  
- **Focus** – you can hide or collapse a list (using the list menu) when you’re not working on that category.  
- **Reporting** – counting cards per list gives a quick health check of each area.

### When to Choose Category Over Stage  

- **Parallel work** – multiple teams are delivering different outputs at the same time.  
- **Non‑linear processes** – tasks may jump between categories without a strict order.  
- **Resource constraints** – you might limit how many cards can sit in a “Resources‑Intensive” list at once.

---

## How Lists Interact with Cards and the Board Overall  

Remember that a **card** lives inside a list. Moving a card from one list to another is the primary way you signal change. Here’s the interaction flow:

1. **Create a card** – it appears in the currently active list.  
2. **Edit the card** – add details, checklists, due dates, etc. (covered later).  
3. **Drag the card** – when you move it to a different list, Trello automatically updates its location on the board.  
4. **Board reflects status** – anyone viewing the board sees the card’s new position, instantly understanding its current stage or category.  

Because lists are part of the board’s structure, any change you make to a list (renaming, reordering, archiving) is visible to everyone with access to the board. This keeps the entire team aligned without the need for separate status meetings.

### Visual Cue: The “Move” Animation  

When you drag a card, Trello shows a smooth slide animation. This visual cue reinforces the idea of “progress” and helps users internalize the workflow.

### Archiving vs. Deleting  

If a list becomes obsolete (e.g., you’ve finished a sprint and no longer need the “Sprint 1” column), you can **archive** it:

1. Click the three‑dot menu on the list header.  
2. Choose **Archive List**.  

Archived lists disappear from the board but remain retrievable from the board’s menu, preserving any cards that might still be needed later. Deleting a list is permanent and should be used only when you’re sure the information is no longer required.

---

## Practical Exercise: Build a Simple Kanban Board  

Let’s put everything together. Assume you’re managing a personal blog launch.

### Step‑by‑Step  

1. **Open your board** (or create a new one named “Blog Launch”).  
2. **Add three lists** named **Ideas**, **Writing**, **Published**.  
3. **Rename** “Ideas” to **Backlog** (use the list menu → Rename).  
4. **Reorder** the lists so they read: **Backlog → Writing → Published**.  
5. **Create three cards**:  
   * “Outline first post” → drop into **Backlog**.  
   * “Draft post on productivity” → drop into **Writing**.  
   * “Publish post on time‑management” → drop into **Published**.  
6. **Drag the “Outline first post” card** from **Backlog** to **Writing** to reflect that you’ve started the draft.  
7. **Observe** how the board now tells the story of your workflow at a glance.

### Reflection Questions  

- Which list name felt most natural for this project?  
- Did reordering the lists change how you thought about the work?  
- How would you separate “Guest Posts” from “Original Content” using lists?

---

## Common Pitfalls & Quick Fixes  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Too many lists** – the board feels crowded. | Over‑categorizing or trying to track every tiny sub‑step. | Consolidate similar categories, or use **labels** on cards for finer granularity. |
| **List names are vague** – “Stuff”, “Later”. | No clear consensus on terminology. | Hold a short team chat to agree on naming conventions; write them down on a “Legend” card. |
| **Cards get stuck** – they never move to the next list. | Lack of clear criteria for “Done”. | Add a **definition of done** in the list description or as a checklist on each card. |
| **Forgot to rename after a sprint** – “Sprint 1” stays after it ends. | Habitual naming without review. | At the end of each sprint, archive the sprint list and create a new one for the next cycle. |

---

## Frequently Asked Questions About Lists  

**Q: Can I have the same list name twice on one board?**  
A: Yes, Trello allows duplicate names, but it can be confusing. It’s best to keep names unique for clarity.

**Q: How many lists can I add?**  
A: Trello imposes no hard limit, but performance may degrade with dozens of lists. If you find the board sluggish, consider splitting the work across multiple boards.

**Q: Do list limits (max cards per list) exist by default?**  
A: List limits are a **Power‑Up** feature. In the core version, you can add as many cards as you like, but you may want to manually enforce a “WIP (work‑in‑progress) limit” by agreeing with your team.

**Q: Can I hide a list without archiving it?**  
A: Not directly, but you can collapse a list using the list menu → **Collapse List** (available on the web and desktop apps). This keeps the list on the board but reduces visual clutter.

---

## Bringing It All Together  

Lists are the scaffolding of your Trello board. By defining clear stages or categories, naming them purposefully, and arranging them in a logical order, you give yourself and anyone else who views the board an instant snapshot of **what needs to happen, where it is, and what’s finished**. As you add cards later, moving them between these lists will become the primary way you signal progress, making the board a living, breathing representation of your workflow.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- A **List** is a vertical column that groups cards by stage, type, or any shared attribute.  
- **Create** a list via the “Add a list” button; **rename** it anytime through the list menu.  
- Choose names that reflect your workflow (e.g., **To Do**, **In Progress**, **Done**) or categories (e.g., **Bugs**, **Features**).  
- **Reorder** lists by dragging the handle; place them in a sequence that mirrors how you think about work.  
- Use lists to **separate task types**, priorities, or time‑based buckets, not just linear stages.  
- Moving a **card** from one list to another updates its status automatically, keeping the whole board synchronized.  
- Keep lists clear, concise, and uniquely named to avoid confusion; regularly review and archive ones that are no longer needed.

modules.title: Adding and Managing Cards: The Heart of Trello Tasks
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Moment: The Launch‑Day Checklist

Imagine you’re the coordinator for a small startup’s product launch. The deadline is Friday, and the team has agreed on three stages of work: **Ideas**, **In Progress**, and **Done**. You’ve already built a board with those three lists, but now you need a way to capture each concrete action—drafting the press release, designing the banner, testing the checkout flow—so nothing slips through the cracks. Each of those actions becomes a **card**, the fundamental unit that turns a vague idea into a trackable task.

---

## Creating Your First Card

1. **Locate the list** where the new task belongs (e.g., *Ideas*).  
2. Click the **“Add a card”** field at the bottom of the list.  
3. Type a concise title (more on naming below) and press **Enter** or **Return**.  

The moment you press Enter, Trello instantly creates a **card** on the board. The card now lives in the chosen list and is ready for additional detail.

> **Why it matters:** A card is the digital equivalent of a sticky note on a physical Kanban board. It is the smallest piece of work you can move, edit, or archive, giving you granular control over every step of your workflow.

---

## Naming Cards Clearly and Concisely

A well‑named card tells you at a glance **what** needs to be done, **who** is responsible (if you include initials), and sometimes **when** it’s due. Follow these quick guidelines:

- **Start with an action verb** – *Write press release*, *Design banner*, *Test checkout*.  
- **Add context only when needed** – *Write press release (Beta version)*.  
- **Keep it short** – Aim for 5‑7 words; longer titles become hard to scan on mobile.  
- **Avoid jargon** that only part of the team understands.  

**Example of a good title:**  
`Create FAQ page – Jane`

**Example of a poor title:**  
`FAQ stuff`

When you consistently apply these naming rules, you’ll find it easier to locate cards, prioritize work, and communicate status to teammates.

---

## Adding Detail to Your Card

A card’s title tells you *what*, but the body of the card holds the *how*, *when*, and *what else*. Below are the three most common details you’ll add during the early phases of a task.

### 1. Description

- Click the card to open the **card detail view**.  
- Select the **“Description”** field and type a brief paragraph or bullet list.  
- Use markdown formatting (e.g., `*` for bullet points) to keep it readable.  

**When to use it:** Capture background information, links to resources, or step‑by‑step instructions. For the launch board, the *Write press release* card might include a link to the brand guidelines and a short brief of the key messages.

### 2. Checklist

A checklist turns a single card into a mini‑project, letting you break a task into subtasks that can be ticked off one by one.

1. Open the card and click **“Checklist”**.  
2. Give the checklist a name (optional) such as *Press Release Draft*.  
3. Add individual items (e.g., *Draft headline*, *Add quotes*, *Proofread*).  

Each checklist item shows a checkbox; clicking it marks the item complete and automatically updates the progress bar on the card front.

**Tip:** If a task has multiple logical groups (e.g., *Content* and *Design*), create separate checklists. This keeps the card organized and gives you a visual cue of which part of the work is lagging.

### 3. Due Date

- In the card detail view, click **“Due Date”**.  
- Choose a calendar date and, if needed, a specific time.  
- Optionally enable a **reminder** (e.g., 1 day before) so you receive an email or push notification.  

The due date appears as a colored badge on the card. Cards whose due dates are approaching turn orange; overdue cards turn red, giving you an at‑a‑glance sense of urgency.

---

## Moving Cards Between Lists to Track Progress

The power of a Kanban board lies in the visual movement of cards from one stage to the next. Here’s how to make that motion smooth:

1. **Drag‑and‑drop** the card from its current list to the target list (e.g., *Ideas → In Progress*).  
2. **Keyboard shortcut**: Click the card, press **`c`** to open the card menu, then **`m`** to bring up the *Move* dialog where you can select the destination list without dragging.  

When you move a card, Trello automatically records the change in the card’s activity log, so you always have a history of who moved what and when.

### Visual Cue: List Colors

If you have applied **background colors** to your lists (a feature introduced earlier), the card retains the same background as the list it resides in. This visual cue reinforces the stage of the workflow at a glance.

### Updating Checklists and Due Dates on the Fly

As a card progresses, you may need to:

- **Add new checklist items** (e.g., after the design is approved, add “Export assets”).  
- **Adjust the due date** if the timeline shifts.  

All edits are saved instantly and reflected on the board, keeping every stakeholder up‑to‑date without the need for separate email threads.

---

## Deleting or Archiving Cards When Tasks Are Completed

Once a task is truly finished, you have two options:

### 1. Archive (the preferred method)

- Open the card and click **“Archive”** at the bottom of the menu.  
- The card disappears from the board but remains in the board’s archive, searchable via the **“Show Menu → Archived Items”** view.  

**Why archive?** It preserves the historical record of what was done, which is useful for post‑mortems or future reference. Archived cards also retain any attached files, comments, and checklists.

### 2. Delete (use sparingly)

- After archiving, open the archived card’s menu and select **“Delete”**.  
- Deleting is permanent; the card and all its content are removed from Trello.  

**When to delete:** Only when the card contains no valuable information (e.g., a placeholder that was never used) or when you need to comply with data‑retention policies.

---

## Maintaining Card Hygiene: Quick Tips

- **Regularly review** the *Ideas* list and archive cards that are no longer relevant.  
- **Consolidate duplicate cards** by merging their checklists and descriptions, then archive the extras.  
- **Use labels** (introduced earlier) to add a quick visual tag—such as “High Priority” or “Waiting on Review”—without cluttering the title.  
- **Limit the number of cards per list** to keep the board scannable; if a list grows beyond 15 cards, consider splitting it into sub‑lists or creating a new board.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Walkthrough

Below is a step‑by‑step illustration of the entire process using our launch‑day scenario.

1. **Add a card** to *Ideas*: `Write press release – Alex`.  
2. **Open the card** and fill in the **Description** with the brief and a link to the brand guide.  
3. **Create a checklist** named *Press Release Draft* with items:  
   - Draft headline  
   - Write body copy  
   - Insert quotes  
   - Proofread  
4. **Set a due date** for **Wednesday, 5 pm** and enable a 1‑day reminder.  
5. **Move the card** to *In Progress* when Alex starts writing.  
6. As Alex checks off each checklist item, the progress bar on the card updates automatically.  
7. **Adjust the due date** to Thursday morning after a minor delay.  
8. Once the press release is approved, **move the card** to *Done*.  
9. **Archive** the card to keep the board tidy while preserving the record of the completed task.

By following these steps, each task becomes a transparent, trackable unit that anyone on the team can understand at a glance.

---

## Key Takeaways

- A **card** is the smallest unit of work on a Trello board; creating one turns an idea into an actionable task.  
- **Clear, concise titles** improve scanability and communication across the team.  
- Adding a **description**, **checklist**, and **due date** supplies the necessary context, sub‑tasks, and timing for each card.  
- **Moving cards** between lists visualizes progress and automatically logs activity.  
- **Archiving** preserves history while keeping the board clean; **deleting** should be reserved for truly unnecessary cards.  

Mastering these card‑level actions equips you to transform any project—from a simple to‑do list to a multi‑phase product launch—into a transparent, manageable workflow.

modules.title: Customizing Cards: Enhancing Tasks with Details and Attachments
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Prompt: Turning a Simple To‑Do Into a Fully‑Featured Card  

Imagine you’re planning a weekend garden party.  
You create a card titled **“Order Fresh Flowers”** on your “Event Planning” board. At first it’s just a line of text, but as the deadline approaches you need to track priority, gather reference images, break the task into steps, and make sure you don’t forget the delivery date. By the end of this chapter you’ll see how the same card can evolve into a miniature command center—complete with **labels**, **attachments**, **checklists**, **due dates**, **reminders**, and a **cover image**—so you can handle any task with the same confidence.

---

## Adding Labels for Instant Visual Cues  

Labels are colored tags that sit on the top‑right of a card. They give you a **quick, at‑a‑glance way to categorize** items without opening the card.

### When to Use Labels  

| Situation | Suggested Label Color | Meaning |
|-----------|----------------------|---------|
| High‑priority tasks | **Red** | Needs immediate attention |
| Items awaiting feedback | **Orange** | Pending review |
| Completed or archived | **Green** | Done, can be archived later |
| Different departments or teams | **Blue, Purple, Yellow** | Separate responsibilities |

You can also **rename** each label (e.g., “Urgent”, “Design”, “Finance”) so the color alone isn’t the only clue.

### Adding a Label – Step by Step  

1. **Hover** over the card (or open it) and click the **Label** icon (a small square).  
2. Choose an existing color or click **“Create a new label”** to pick a fresh hue.  
3. Type a name for the label (optional but recommended for beginners).  
4. Press **Enter** to apply. The label appears on the card front‑and‑center.

### Editing or Removing Labels  

- **Edit**: Click the label again, change its name or color, then save.  
- **Remove**: Click the **X** on the label badge, or deselect the color in the label menu.

**Tip:** Use the board’s **filter** button (top‑right) to show only cards with a certain label. This is handy when you want to see all “Urgent” items across multiple lists.

---

## Attaching Files, Images, and Links  

Attachments turn a card into a **reference hub**. Whether it’s a PDF brief, a photo of a design mock‑up, or a link to a shared Google Sheet, everything you need lives right where the task lives.

### Types of Attachments  

- **Local files** – PDFs, Word docs, spreadsheets, images, etc.  
- **Cloud files** – Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Box.  
- **Web links** – URLs to articles, videos, or project management tools.  

### Adding an Attachment  

1. Open the card (click the title).  
2. Click **“Attachment”** (paperclip icon).  
3. Choose the source: **Computer**, **Google Drive**, **Dropbox**, **OneDrive**, **Box**, or **Link**.  
4. Select the file or paste the URL, then click **Open** or **Attach**.  

The attachment appears in the card’s **Attachments** section, with a thumbnail for images and a file‑type icon for documents.

### Managing Attachments  

- **Rename**: Click the attachment’s name, edit, and press **Enter**.  
- **Delete**: Hover over the attachment and click the **trash can** icon.  
- **Download**: Click the attachment to open it, then use the download option in the viewer.

**Tip:** Drag an image attachment onto the card’s **cover area** (see the “Cover Images” section) to instantly turn it into a visual header.

---

## Building Checklists for Multi‑Step Tasks  

A checklist is a **mini‑to‑do list** inside a card. It’s perfect for breaking down a complex task—like “Order Fresh Flowers”—into manageable steps.

### Creating a Checklist  

1. Open the card and click **“Checklist”**.  
2. Give the checklist a name (e.g., “Flower Order Steps”).  
3. Press **Enter** to add the checklist container.  

### Adding Items  

- Type an item (e.g., “Select bouquet style”) and press **Enter**.  
- Continue adding as many items as needed.

### Using Checklist Features  

- **Check off** items by clicking the box; the progress bar at the top of the checklist updates automatically.  
- **Reorder** items by dragging the three‑dot handle.  
- **Copy** a checklist to another card via the card’s **“More”** menu → **“Copy checklist”**.  

### Advanced Checklist Tips  

- **Assign items**: While Trello doesn’t natively assign checklist items, you can **mention** a teammate in the item’s description (e.g., “@Anna – confirm colors”).  
- **Add due dates**: For critical steps, create a **sub‑card** (via the “Add Card” button inside the checklist) and set its own due date.

---

## Setting Due Dates and Reminders  

Due dates keep your tasks **time‑bound**. Trello’s built‑in calendar shows all cards with dates, and you can receive **email or push notifications** as deadlines approach.

### Adding a Due Date  

1. Open the card and click the **Calendar** icon (looks like a small calendar).  
2. Choose a date from the pop‑up calendar.  
3. (Optional) Add a specific **time** for more precise alerts.  
4. Click **“Save”**. The date appears on the card front‑and‑center.

### Configuring Reminders  

- After setting a due date, a **“Set Reminder”** dropdown appears. Choose **“10 minutes before”**, **“1 hour before”**, **“1 day before”**, or **“Custom”**.  
- Reminders are sent via the notification system you’ve configured in your **profile settings** (email, mobile push, or desktop).

### Viewing All Due Dates  

- Click the **Calendar** view button at the top of the board to see a month‑grid of every card with a due date.  
- Use the **“Search Cards”** field and type `due:today` or `due:next week` to filter cards by upcoming deadlines.

**Tip:** If a card’s due date passes without completion, Trello automatically highlights the date in **red**, giving you an immediate visual cue that the task is overdue.

---

## Using Card Cover Images to Highlight Important Tasks  

A **cover image** is a large visual banner that sits at the top of a card. It can be a photo, a color block, or even a custom graphic. Covers make high‑visibility cards stand out in a crowded list.

### Adding a Cover Image  

1. Open the card and click **“Cover”** (paint‑brush icon).  
2. Choose one of the following sources:  
   - **Upload** an image from your computer.  
   - **Select** an existing attachment (image) on the card.  
   - **Pick** a solid color (good for quick visual tags).  
3. Adjust the **display mode**:  
   - **“Full”** – image stretches across the card width.  
   - **“Fit”** – image shows in a smaller thumbnail.  
   - **“Cover”** – image appears as a background behind the card’s title.  

### Updating or Removing a Cover  

- To **change** the cover, repeat the steps above and select a new image or color.  
- To **remove**, click the **X** next to the current cover in the Cover menu.

### Practical Use Cases  

- **Project milestones** – use a bold color or a milestone icon as the cover.  
- **Brand assets** – attach a logo image as the cover for design‑related cards.  
- **Mood boards** – set a photo of a finished product as the cover to inspire the team.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Walkthrough  

Let’s revisit the “Order Fresh Flowers” card and apply every feature we’ve covered.

1. **Label** – Apply a **Red** label named “Urgent”.  
2. **Attachment** – Upload a PDF of the florist’s price list and attach a link to the online order form.  
3. **Cover** – Choose the florist’s logo from the attachments as a **Full** cover image.  
4. **Checklist** – Create a checklist called “Order Steps” with items:  
   - Select bouquet style  
   - Confirm budget with finance  
   - Place order on the website  
   - Verify delivery address  
5. **Due Date** – Set the due date to **Friday, 5 pm** (the day before the party).  
6. **Reminder** – Choose “1 hour before” so you receive a push notification when the deadline is near.  

Now, when you glance at the board, the red label and vibrant cover instantly signal priority, the checklist shows progress (e.g., 2 of 4 items checked), and the due‑date badge reminds you of the looming deadline. If you need more detail, just open the card and you’ll find the price list, the order link, and any comments from teammates.

---

## Best Practices for Beginner Card Customization  

- **Start simple**: Add one label, one attachment, and a short checklist before layering more features.  
- **Use colors consistently**: Pick a color code (e.g., Red = High priority) and stick to it across all boards.  
- **Keep attachments lean**: Large files can slow down board loading; consider linking to cloud‑hosted files instead of uploading heavy PDFs.  
- **Leverage the calendar view**: Periodically switch to Calendar mode to verify that due dates are realistic and evenly distributed.  
- **Refresh cover images**: Update covers when a task transitions from “Planning” to “In Progress” to keep visual cues aligned with the task’s status.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can a card have more than one label?**  
A: Yes. You can apply up to **six** labels per card, each with its own color and name.

**Q: Will my attachments count against my storage limit?**  
A: Attachments stored on Trello count toward the board’s storage quota (10 GB for free accounts). Using linked cloud files bypasses this limit.

**Q: How do I see who added a checklist item?**  
A: The checklist itself doesn’t track authorship, but you can add a **comment** right after checking an item to note who completed it.

**Q: Can I set a different reminder for each checklist item?**  
A: Not directly. Create a **sub‑card** for each critical checklist item and set its own due date and reminder.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Labels** provide instant visual categorization; use colors and names consistently.  
- **Attachments** centralize reference material—choose the most appropriate source (local file, cloud, or link).  
- **Checklists** break complex tasks into actionable steps and display progress at a glance.  
- **Due dates** and **reminders** keep tasks time‑bound and ensure you receive timely alerts.  
- **Cover images** turn a card into a visual focal point, helping priority tasks stand out.  

By mastering these card‑customization tools, you transform a simple list entry into a comprehensive, self‑contained task hub—exactly the kind of organized workflow Trello promises.

modules.title: Collaboration in Trello: Working with Teams and Guests
modules.content:
## Bringing Others Onto Your Board  

Imagine you’re planning a weekend charity bake‑sale. You’ve already built a board with lists for **Ideas**, **Shopping**, **Baking**, and **Day‑of Tasks**. The next step is to get the volunteers—your cousin, the local bakery, and a friend who will handle social media—into the same visual workspace so everyone knows who is doing what.  

In Trello, collaboration starts with **inviting** people. You can add them by email address or generate a shareable link. The process is the same whether the board is private (only invited members can see it) or team‑visible (anyone on your Trello team can join).  

### 1. Inviting Team Members  

1. Open the board you want to share.  
2. Click the **Invite** button at the top of the board (the little person‑plus‑icon).  
3. In the dialog that appears, type the email address of the person you’d like to add.  
   * If the person already has a Trello account, they will be added instantly.  
   * If they don’t, Trello will send them an invitation email with a link to create an account.  
4. Press **Send Invitation**.  

The invited person now appears in the **Members** area of the board header, and their avatar shows up on any card they’re assigned to.

### 2. Inviting Guests  

Sometimes you need to collaborate with someone outside your organization—say, a freelance designer. Trello calls these participants **Guests**. Guests can be added the same way you add team members, but you have the option to limit what they can do.

1. Follow steps 1‑3 above.  
2. After typing the email, click the **gear icon** next to the email field.  
3. Choose a permission level for the guest (see the **Set Permissions** section below).  
4. Send the invitation.  

Guests receive the same email invitation, but their access respects the limits you set.

### 3. Sharing a Link  

If you prefer not to type email addresses, you can generate a **shareable link**:

1. Click the **Invite** button.  
2. At the bottom of the invitation dialog, select **Create a link**.  
3. Choose the default permission for anyone who uses the link (member, comment‑only, or view‑only).  
4. Copy the link and paste it into a chat, email, or Slack channel.  

Anyone with the link can join the board according to the permission you selected. This method is handy for ad‑hoc collaborations or for quickly onboarding a group of volunteers.

---

## Assigning Responsibility With Card Members  

A board shows the big picture, but the **cards** hold the actionable work. Assigning a member to a card makes it clear who owns a task, and the assigned member’s avatar appears on the front of the card—visible to everyone at a glance.

### How to Add a Member to a Card  

1. Open the card you want to assign.  
2. Click the **Members** button (the silhouette icon) on the right‑hand side of the card back.  
3. Select one or more people from the list that appears.  
   * If the person isn’t already a board member, you can type their email to invite them directly from this view.  
4. The avatars appear on the card front.  

You can add or remove members at any time, which is useful when responsibilities shift during a project.

### Best Practices for Assignment  

- **One primary owner**: Choose a single “owner” for each card to avoid confusion.  
- **Secondary collaborators**: Add others as secondary members when they need to review or contribute.  
- **Use Labels for roles**: Complement member assignments with colored **Labels** (e.g., “Design”, “Copy”) to visualize workload distribution across the board.  

---

## Communicating Directly on Cards  

When a card lives on a board, the **Comments** section becomes the conversation hub. Instead of sending separate emails or messages, keep all discussion attached to the task it concerns.

### Posting a Comment  

1. Open the card.  
2. Scroll to the **Comment** field at the bottom.  
3. Type your message and press **Enter** or click **Save**.  

Your comment appears in a chronological feed, and anyone who can view the card can read it. Comments support **@mentions**, **attachments**, and **emoji**, making them a flexible communication tool.

### Using @mentions  

An **@mention** notifies a specific person (or the whole board) that they have been referenced.  

- **Syntax**: Type `@` followed by the person’s name or username. Trello will show a dropdown of matching members; click the correct one.  
- **Effect**: The mentioned person receives a notification (via email, mobile push, or in‑app) and the comment is highlighted with their name.  

**Example**:  

> “@Alex, could you add the final budget spreadsheet to this card? Thanks!”  

When Alex reads the comment, the mention draws immediate attention, and the task becomes clearer.

### Commenting in Descriptions  

Sometimes you want a note that stays visible even when the card is collapsed. The **Description** field is ideal for static information, but you can still embed @mentions there.  

- Edit the description, type `@` and select a member.  
- Save the changes.  

The mentioned person will be notified, and the note remains at the top of the card, visible to anyone who opens it.

### Thread‑Like Organization  

While Trello does not have nested comment threads, you can simulate a conversation flow:

- **Quote** previous comments by copying the text and prefixing it with `>` (Markdown blockquote).  
- **Timestamp** key updates manually (e.g., “**2024‑08‑09** – Final design approved”).  

These conventions help readers follow the evolution of a discussion without getting lost.

---

## Setting Permissions: Controlling What Others Can Do  

Not every collaborator needs the same level of access. Trello offers three primary permission tiers per board:

| Permission | What the user can do |
|------------|----------------------|
| **View‑only** | Browse the board and read cards, but cannot add comments, edit cards, or move items. |
| **Comment‑only** | View the board and add comments, but cannot change card titles, due dates, or move cards. |
| **Edit (Member)** | Full access: add, edit, move cards, assign members, and adjust board settings (except admin‑only actions). |

### Adjusting Permissions for an Individual  

1. Open the board menu (the three‑dot icon at the top right).  
2. Choose **Settings** → **Permissions**.  
3. Locate the member you want to modify in the **Members** list.  
4. Click the dropdown next to their name and select the desired permission level.  

Changes take effect immediately. For guests, the same dropdown appears when you invite them or later from the **Members** list.

### Setting Default Permissions for Link Sharing  

When you generate a shareable link (see earlier), you also decide the default permission for anyone who joins via that link. This is useful for:

- **Open brainstorming sessions** – give “Comment‑only” access so participants can suggest ideas without rearranging cards.  
- **Stakeholder reviews** – use “View‑only” to let executives see progress without risking accidental edits.  

Remember that you can still upgrade or downgrade individual members after they join, regardless of the link’s default setting.

---

## Practical Workflow: From Invitation to Completion  

Below is a step‑by‑step illustration of how a small team might use the features covered in this chapter to manage a project.

### Scenario: Launching a Community Newsletter  

| Step | Action | Trello Feature |
|------|--------|----------------|
| 1 | **Create board** “Community Newsletter – July”. | Board (already covered). |
| 2 | **Invite** the editor, graphic designer, and a guest copywriter. | Invite by email; set guest to “Comment‑only”. |
| 3 | **Add cards** for each article idea in the “Ideas” list. | Cards (previous chapter). |
| 4 | **Assign** the editor to the “Finalize Layout” card. | Card Members. |
| 5 | **Comment** on the “Interview with Mayor” card: “@Copywriter, can you draft the interview questions?” | Comments + @mentions. |
| 6 | **Copywriter** replies in the same comment thread, attaching a draft document. | Attachments in comments. |
| 7 | **Editor** changes the card’s permission to “Edit” for the copywriter once the draft is approved. | Adjusting permissions. |
| 8 | **Graphic designer** moves the “Create Infographic” card from “To‑Do” to “In‑Progress”. | Card movement (requires edit permission). |
| 9 | **Stakeholder** receives a view‑only link to the board to monitor progress without altering anything. | Shareable link with view‑only permission. |
|10 | **All members** check the board each morning; completed cards are moved to “Done”. | Visual workflow. |

Through this flow, every participant knows their responsibilities, receives timely notifications via @mentions, and works within the permission boundaries you set.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Collaboration Hurdles  

| Issue | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|-------|--------------|-----------|
| *Member can’t see a card they were assigned to.* | The board is **private** and the member wasn’t added to the board. | Invite the person to the board first, then assign the card. |
| *Guest receives “You don’t have permission to comment” error.* | Guest was given **view‑only** permission. | Upgrade their permission to “Comment‑only” or “Edit” from the Members list. |
| *@mention doesn’t trigger a notification.* | The mentioned name isn’t a board member (e.g., typo or external email). | Ensure the person is added to the board; if not, invite them. |
| *Accidental card move wipes out a workflow.* | A member with edit rights moved a card to the wrong list. | Use the board’s **Activity** log to locate the move, then drag the card back. |
| *Too many notifications from a busy board.* | Everyone is set to “Edit” and receives updates for every change. | Adjust individual notification settings in **Settings → Notifications**, or limit the number of members with edit rights. |

---

## Tips for Smooth Team Collaboration  

- **Name your members clearly**: Trello displays the avatar and the name you see in the board header. Encourage teammates to use their full names or recognizable nicknames to avoid confusion in @mentions.  
- **Use a “Team” list**: Create a list called **Team** that contains a card for each member with their contact details, preferred communication channels, and role. This serves as a quick reference.  
- **Set a “Board Etiquette” card**: Outline expectations for comment frequency, response time, and permission usage. Pin this card to the top of a “Guidelines” list so it’s always visible.  
- **Leverage the “Watch” feature**: If a member only needs updates on specific cards, they can click **Watch** (the eye icon) on those cards to receive notifications without being a board member.  
- **Regularly review permissions**: At the start of each major phase, check the **Members** list to confirm that each person still has the appropriate level of access.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can I invite someone using only their Slack username?**  
A: Direct Slack integration is a Power‑Up (covered later). For now, invitations must be sent via email or a shareable link.

**Q: What happens if a guest leaves the organization?**  
A: Their access remains until you remove them manually from the board’s Members list. It’s good practice to audit guest accounts quarterly.

**Q: Are there limits on how many members a board can have?**  
A: Free Trello boards can have up to 10 members. Paid plans raise this limit. Guest accounts count toward the same limit.

**Q: How do I know who has viewed a card?**  
A: Trello does not currently track view activity. You can ask members to **comment** when they’ve reviewed a card, or use the “Watch” feature to see when a card is updated.

---

## Bringing It All Together  

Collaboration in Trello hinges on three simple actions:

1. **Invite** the right people with the appropriate permission level.  
2. **Assign** cards so ownership is crystal‑clear.  
3. **Communicate** through comments and @mentions, keeping the conversation attached to the work itself.  

When these steps are combined with thoughtful board organization—lists that reflect your workflow, labels that highlight roles, and clear etiquette—you create a shared space where every participant can see, contribute, and stay aligned without endless email threads.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- Invite teammates or external guests via **email** or **shareable link**; set their permission (view, comment, edit) at the moment of invitation.  
- Assign members to cards to indicate responsibility; avatars on the card front give instant visual cues.  
- Use **Comments** for updates, questions, and decisions; embed **@mentions** to notify specific people.  
- Adjust **board permissions** per member or per link to control what collaborators can do.  
- @mentions work both in comments and in card descriptions, ensuring important notes trigger notifications.  
- Regularly audit members and permissions to keep the board secure and efficient.  

By mastering these collaboration tools, you turn a static Kanban board into a living, shared workspace that keeps every team member on the same page—no matter where they are.

modules.title: Automating Trello: Using Butler to Save Time
modules.content:
## Meet Butler: Trello’s Built‑in Automation Engine  

Imagine you’ve just set up a board for your personal project‑management system. You’ve created **Lists** for “Backlog,” “In Progress,” and “Done,” and you’ve started adding **Cards** with due dates, checklists, and labels. After a few days you notice a repetitive pattern: every morning you move any card whose due date is today from “Backlog” to “In Progress,” and at night you archive any card that is marked **Done**. Doing this manually takes a few minutes each day—minutes that add up over weeks and months.

**Butler** is Trello’s native automation tool that can perform those repetitive actions for you, freeing up mental space for the work that truly matters. It works by listening for triggers (e.g., “a card is moved,” “the due date arrives”) and then executing predefined actions (e.g., “move the card to another list,” “add a label”). Because Butler lives inside Trello, you never need to install a separate extension or learn a new programming language; you build automation through a series of simple, visual steps.

> **Key point:** Butler = **Trigger + Action**. Think of each rule as “When X happens, do Y.”

---

## Why Automate? The Time‑Saving Benefits  

| Repetitive task | Manual effort (per occurrence) | Potential automation | Time saved per week* |
|-----------------|-------------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Move cards whose due date is today | 10 seconds | Auto‑move on due date | ~2 minutes |
| Add a “Late” label when a card is overdue | 8 seconds | Auto‑label overdue cards | ~1.5 minutes |
| Archive cards marked Done at day‑end | 12 seconds | Auto‑archive at 6 pm | ~2 minutes |

\*Assumes 10 occurrences of each task per week. The numbers are illustrative, not exact.

Even modest savings become significant when you manage multiple boards or large projects. Butler also helps maintain consistency—rules are applied the same way every time, reducing human error.

---

## Getting Started: Where Butler Lives  

1. **Open a board** you want to automate.  
2 **Locate the Butler button** in the board header (right‑hand side, next to Power‑Ups). It appears as a magic‑wand icon.  
3. **Click the icon** to open the Butler panel. The panel has four tabs:  
   - **Rules** – trigger‑based automations that run automatically.  
   - **Card Buttons** – buttons you can add to any card to run a command on demand.  
   - **Board Buttons** – buttons that sit at the top of the board for one‑click actions.  
   - **Scheduled Commands** – actions that run at a specific time or recurring interval.

The first three tabs (Rules, Card Buttons, Board Buttons) are *event‑driven*; the fourth is *time‑driven*. For beginners, we’ll focus on **Rules** and **Scheduled Commands**, as they cover the most common “set‑and‑forget” needs.

---

## Simple Rule: Auto‑Move Cards When the Due Date Arrives  

### Scenario  
You run a weekly content calendar. Each Monday you create a card for the article to be published that week, set the due date to Thursday, and place the card in the “Ideas” list. When Thursday arrives, you want the card to automatically jump to the “Ready to Publish” list so you can focus on the final touches.

### Step‑by‑Step  

1. **Open the Butler panel** → **Rules** tab.  
2. Click **“Create Rule.”**  
3. **Choose a trigger:**  
   - Click **“When a card is due.”**  
   - A dropdown appears; select **“the due date is today.”**  
4. **Add an action:**  
   - Click **“Add Action.”**  
   - Choose **“Move the card to list…”** → select **“Ready to Publish.”**  
5. **Name the rule** (optional but helpful). Example: *“Move due cards to Ready to Publish.”*  
6. **Save** the rule.

From now on, any card whose due date matches the current day will instantly relocate to the “Ready to Publish” list, no matter which list it started in.

> **Tip:** If you have multiple boards with similar workflows, you can **copy** a rule from one board to another via the three‑dot menu on the rule card.

---

## Adding a Second Simple Rule: Auto‑Label Overdue Cards  

A common pain point is spotting overdue items. Rather than scanning every list, let Butler add a red **“Late”** label automatically.

### Steps  

1. In the **Rules** tab, click **“Create Rule.”**  
2. **Trigger:** *“When a card becomes overdue.”* (Butler provides this trigger directly.)  
3. **Action:** *“Add the red label ‘Late’ to the card.”*  
4. **Save** the rule.

Now any card that passes its due date receives a visual cue—your red label—making it impossible to miss.

---

## Custom Commands: Tailoring Automation to Your Workflow  

While the built‑in triggers cover many scenarios, Butler also lets you craft **custom commands** that combine several actions. This is useful when you want a single button to do multiple things at once.

### Example: “Start Sprint” Card Button  

You manage a software development board with the lists **Backlog**, **Sprint**, and **Done**. When a sprint begins, you want to:

1. Move all cards with the label **“Sprint‑Ready”** from **Backlog** to **Sprint**.  
2. Add a **“Sprint 1”** label to each moved card.  
3. Set the due date of each card to the sprint’s end date (e.g., 14 days from today).

#### Building the Card Button  

1. Open Butler → **Card Buttons** tab.  
2. Click **“Create Card Button.”**  
3. **Name the button:** *“Start Sprint.”*  
4. **Add actions** (in order):  

   - **“Find all cards in list ‘Backlog’ with label ‘Sprint‑Ready’.”**  
   - **“Move the found cards to list ‘Sprint’.”**  
   - **“Add label ‘Sprint 1’ to the found cards.”**  
   - **“Set due date of the found cards to 14 days from now.”**  

5. **Save** the button.

When you click the **Start Sprint** button on any card (or on the board’s card‑button area), Butler will execute the four actions in sequence, instantly reshaping your board for the new sprint.

> **Note:** Custom commands can reference **variables** such as `{cardname}` or `{date}`. This lets you personalize messages in comments or checklists, e.g., “Added to Sprint 1 on {date}”.

---

## Using Butler Templates: Jump‑Start Common Automation Scenarios  

Butler includes a library of **templates**—pre‑built rule sets for frequent use cases. Templates save you the time of building each rule from scratch and also expose you to advanced techniques you might not think of.

### How to Access Templates  

1. In the Butler panel, click the **“Templates”** link at the bottom of any tab (Rules, Card Buttons, etc.).  
2. Browse categories such as **“Project Management,” “Personal Productivity,” “Team Collaboration.”**  
3. Click a template to preview its triggers and actions.  
4. Hit **“Add to Board”** to import the whole set onto your current board.

### Three Handy Templates for Beginners  

| Template | What It Does | Typical Use |
|----------|--------------|-------------|
| **Card Aging** | Moves cards that haven’t been updated in 7 days to an “Aging” list and adds a “Stale” label. | Keeps long‑standing items visible. |
| **Daily Summary** | At 9 am, posts a comment on a designated “Dashboard” card listing all cards due today. | Gives you a quick daily briefing. |
| **Checklist Completion** | When a checklist on a card is marked complete, automatically moves the card to “Done.” | Streamlines task finalization. |

After adding a template, you can **modify** any rule to better fit your board (e.g., change the list names or time intervals). Think of templates as a scaffold you can customize.

---

## Scheduled Commands: Time‑Based Automation  

Sometimes you need actions that run **regardless of card activity**, such as sending a weekly reminder or cleaning up old cards. Butler’s **Scheduled Commands** let you set up cron‑style schedules without any coding.

### Example: Weekly “Review” Reminder  

You want a reminder every Monday at 9 am that prompts the team to review the “In Review” list.

#### Steps  

1. In Butler → **Scheduled Commands** tab, click **“Create Command.”**  
2. **Set the schedule:** Choose **“Every Monday at 09:00.”**  
3. **Select an action:** *“Post comment ‘Please review cards in the In Review list.’ on the card ‘Weekly Review.’”*  
4. **Save** the command.

Each Monday, the designated card will receive the comment, serving as a gentle nudge for the team.

> **Pro tip:** Use the **“@team”** mention in comments to notify all board members instantly.

---

## Enabling and Disabling Automation Safely  

Automation is powerful, but there are moments when you need to pause it—perhaps during a major board restructure or while troubleshooting unexpected behavior. Butler gives you granular control.

### Board‑Level Toggle  

- At the top of the Butler panel, there’s a **switch** labeled **“Automation on this board.”** Turning it **off** disables **all** Butler rules, buttons, and scheduled commands for that board. Existing cards remain unchanged; only future triggers are ignored.

### Individual Rule Toggle  

- Each rule, button, or scheduled command has a **three‑dot menu** (⋮). Selecting **“Disable”** pauses only that specific automation while leaving the rest active. You can later **“Enable”** it again with a single click.

### Best Practices  

- **Label your rules** clearly (e.g., “Auto‑move due cards – active”) so you can spot which ones are enabled.  
- **Test a new rule on a dummy card** before applying it to real work items.  
- **Document** any disabled automation in the board’s description or a dedicated “Automation Log” card, noting why it was turned off and when you plan to reactivate it.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Project Walkthrough  

Let’s combine the concepts into a cohesive workflow for a **freelance designer** who tracks client projects on a single board.

### Board Layout  

- **Lists:** “Ideas,” “Design,” “Review,” “Ready to Deliver,” “Done.”  
- **Labels:** Red “Late,” Green “Approved,” Blue “Client X,” etc.  

### Desired Automations  

1. **When a card’s due date arrives, move it to “Ready to Deliver.”**  
2. **If a card becomes overdue, add the red “Late” label.**  
3. **When the “Review” checklist is completed, move the card to “Ready to Deliver” and add the green “Approved” label.**  
4. **Every Friday at 5 pm, post a summary comment on a “Weekly Summary” card listing all cards still in “Design.”**  

### Implementation  

| Step | Butler Feature | Action |
|------|----------------|--------|
| 1 | **Rule** (due‑date trigger) | “When a card is due today, move it to list ‘Ready to Deliver.’” |
| 2 | **Rule** (overdue trigger) | “When a card becomes overdue, add red label ‘Late.’” |
| 3 | **Card Button** (custom) | Create a button named “Mark Approved” that (a) checks if the “Review” checklist is complete, (b) moves the card to “Ready to Deliver,” and (c) adds the green “Approved” label. |
| 4 | **Scheduled Command** | “Every Friday at 17:00, post comment ‘Design list status: {cards in list “Design”}’ on card ‘Weekly Summary.’” |

After setting up these four automations, the designer’s board runs itself: overdue tasks are flagged, completed designs automatically progress, and a weekly snapshot keeps the client in the loop without manual effort.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Rule fires too early** (e.g., moving a card before the due date) | Using “due in X days” instead of “due today.” | Double‑check trigger wording; choose “the due date is today.” |
| **Too many rules cause performance lag** | Each board has a quota of **automation actions per month** (free tier: 250 actions). | Prioritize essential rules; combine actions where possible; monitor usage in Butler’s **“Usage”** tab. |
| **Unexpected side effects** (e.g., a rule moving a card that another rule also moves) | Overlapping triggers without clear ordering. | Use **“Only when”** conditions to narrow scope, or disable one rule while testing the other. |
| **Automation stops after board rename** | Some rules reference list names; renaming a list breaks the reference. | Use **list IDs** (Butler automatically updates when you rename a list) or edit the rule after renaming. |
| **Scheduled command never runs** | Timezone mismatch or board not active. | Verify the board’s **timezone setting** (Board Settings → General) and ensure the board is not archived. |

---

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)  

**Q: Do Butler rules run instantly?**  
A: Yes. When the trigger condition is met, Butler executes the rule within a few seconds. For scheduled commands, execution occurs at the exact minute specified.

**Q: Can I share my custom commands with teammates?**  
A: Absolutely. When you create a rule or button, it lives on the board, so anyone with access can use it. You can also **export** a rule (three‑dot menu → “Export”) and import it into another board.

**Q: What happens if a rule exceeds my monthly action quota?**  
A: The rule will stop executing until the next month or until you upgrade to a higher plan. Butler will notify you in the panel when you approach the limit.

**Q: Is Butler available on mobile?**  
A: Yes. The Butler panel appears in the mobile app’s board menu, though some advanced features (like templates) may be easier to manage from a desktop browser.

---

## Next Steps
