- **Experiment**: Add a simple “when a card is added, assign it to you” rule and watch it work.  
- **Explore Templates**: Try the “Card Aging” template to see how Butler can surface forgotten tasks.  
- **Scale Up**: As you become comfortable, combine multiple actions into a single custom command to handle more complex workflows.

By mastering Butler, you turn Trello from a static visual board into a dynamic, self‑maintaining system that does the heavy lifting for you.

## Key Takeaways  

- **Butler = Trigger + Action**; it automates repetitive board activities without any coding.  
- Simple rules (e.g., auto‑move cards on due date) can be built in a few clicks.  
- **Custom commands** let you bundle several actions into one button, tailoring automation to your exact workflow.  
- **Templates** provide ready‑made rule sets for common scenarios; they can be customized after import.  
- **Scheduled commands** run at specific times, perfect for weekly reminders or clean‑up tasks.  
- You can **enable/disable** automation at the board level or per rule, allowing safe experimentation and troubleshooting.  
- Monitoring action quotas and avoiding overlapping triggers keeps Butler running smoothly.  

With Butler in your toolbox, you’ll spend less time clicking and more time delivering results.

modules.title: Power-Ups: Extending Trello with Third-Party Integrations
modules.content:
## What Are Power‑Ups?

Imagine you have a **digital Kanban board** that already shows your tasks, due dates, and team comments. Now you want the board to automatically add a meeting to your Google Calendar every time you set a due date, or to post a notification in Slack the moment a card moves from “In Progress” to “Done.”  
That extra capability is what Trello calls a **Power‑Up**.

A Power‑Up is a plug‑in that connects Trello to another service—or adds a new feature that Trello doesn’t provide out of the box. Think of it as a small app that lives inside your board, giving you access to tools you already use (e.g., Google Drive) or new visualizations (e.g., a Calendar view). Because Power‑Ups sit on top of the board you already built in earlier chapters, they let you keep your familiar workflow while extending its power.

### Why Power‑Ups Matter

| Situation | Trello alone | With a Power‑Up |
|-----------|--------------|-----------------|
| Need to see all due dates on a calendar | Scroll through each list and card | Calendar view shows every card with a date in one glance |
| Want to share a file stored in Google Drive | Attach the file manually, no live link | Google Drive Power‑Up creates a live link and syncs changes |
| Team communicates in Slack | Mention “@team” in a comment, no automatic notification | Slack Power‑Up posts a message whenever a card is updated |

By adding only the Power‑Ups you truly need, you can keep your board clean, reduce context‑switching, and let the tools you already love work together seamlessly.

---

## Finding the Right Power‑Ups for Your Workflow

### The Power‑Up Directory

Trello hosts a **Power‑Up Directory** that you can reach from any board:

1. Open the board where you want to add a Power‑Up.  
2. Click the **“Power‑Ups”** button in the board menu (the vertical list on the right).  
3. A searchable gallery appears, grouped by categories such as *Productivity*, *Reporting*, *File Management*, and *Communication*.

Each entry shows a short description, an icon, and whether the Power‑Up is free, paid, or offers a free tier.

### Selecting a Power‑Up

When you browse the directory, ask yourself:

- **Do I already use this external service?** If you already have a Google account, the Google Drive Power‑Up will feel familiar.  
- **Will this Power‑Up solve a specific pain point?** For example, if you frequently miss deadlines, the Calendar Power‑Up gives you a visual overview.  
- **What are the cost and permission implications?** Some Power‑Ups require admin rights on the external service (e.g., Slack) or charge per user after a free trial.

Pick one or two to start; you can always add more later.

---

## Getting Started with Three Popular Power‑Ups

Below are step‑by‑step guides for three of the most frequently used Power‑Ups. Each guide assumes you have a board already created (see Chapters 1‑4).

### Calendar Power‑Up

The Calendar Power‑Up turns due dates on your cards into calendar events, and it can sync with external calendars like Google Calendar.

#### Enable the Calendar Power‑Up

1. Open your board, click **Power‑Ups** in the right‑hand menu.  
2. Search for **“Calendar”** and click **Add**.  
3. The Power‑Up appears as a new button at the top of the board labeled **Calendar**.

#### Sync with Google Calendar

1. Click the **Calendar** button, then choose **Settings** (gear icon).  
2. Select **“Enable Google Calendar Sync.”**  
3. You’ll be prompted to sign into your Google account and grant Trello permission to read and write calendar events.  
4. Choose which Trello board(s) to sync and pick a destination Google Calendar (you can create a dedicated “Trello Board” calendar if you like).  
5. Click **Save**.  

Now every card with a due date automatically appears as an event in the selected Google Calendar. If you edit the date in Trello, the change propagates to Google Calendar within a few minutes, and vice‑versa.

### Slack Power‑Up

If your team lives in Slack, this Power‑Up keeps everyone in the loop without leaving Trello.

#### Connect Slack to Trello

1. In the **Power‑Ups** menu, search for **“Slack.”** Click **Add**.  
2. A dialog asks you to **“Connect to Slack.”** Click the button and sign into your Slack workspace.  
3. Authorize Trello to post messages on your behalf.  

#### Using the Slack Power‑Up

- **Automatic notifications:** In the Power‑Up settings, toggle on *“When a card is moved to Done, post to #project‑updates.”*  
- **Manual posting:** Open any card, click the **Slack** button, type a short message, and select the channel where it should appear.  
- **Link back:** The posted Slack message includes a link that takes you directly to the Trello card, making follow‑up easy.

### Google Drive Power‑Up

Storing files in the cloud is common; the Google Drive Power‑Up lets you attach Drive files without leaving Trello.

#### Attach a Drive File

1. Add the **Google Drive** Power‑Up from the directory.  
2. Open a card, click **“Attach File”**, and choose the **Google Drive** tab.  
3. Browse your Drive, select a file, and click **Attach**.  

The attachment appears on the card as a live link. If the file is edited in Drive, the link on the card automatically reflects the latest version—no need to re‑upload.

#### Quick tip: Embed Docs

When you attach a Google Doc, you can click **“Open in new tab”** or **“Preview”** directly from the card. This preview shows the most recent content, letting you skim a document without opening Drive.

---

## Configuring Power‑Ups on Your Board

### Accessing Board Settings

Every Power‑Up you add creates a **Settings** button (usually a gear icon) next to its name on the board toolbar. Clicking it opens a modal where you can:

- Choose which lists or cards the Power‑Up applies to.  
- Set up integration details (e.g., which Slack channel to post to).  
- Define permissions for board members (who can edit the Power‑Up’s configuration).

### Adjusting Permissions

Power‑Ups often need broader access than a regular board member. For example, the Google Drive Power‑Up requires the board admin to grant Trello permission to view your Drive files. If you’re not the board admin, you’ll see a prompt asking the admin to approve the connection.

**Best practice:** Keep the list of users who can change Power‑Up settings short—typically the board owner and a designated “Power‑Up Manager.” This prevents accidental disconnections.

### Adding Custom Fields (Optional)

Some Power‑Ups, like the **Custom Fields** Power‑Up, let you create extra data columns on cards (e.g., “Budget” or “Priority”). To add it:

1. Open **Power‑Ups**, search for **“Custom Fields.”**  
2. Click **Add**, then click **“Add a field”** on any card to define the field type (text, number, dropdown, etc.).  

Custom fields can be used in combination with other Power‑Ups—for instance, you could filter a Calendar view by a “Project Phase” custom field.

---

## Managing Power‑Ups Over Time

### When to Disable or Remove a Power‑Up

Power‑Ups are useful, but each one adds a small amount of loading time and can clutter the board interface. Consider disabling a Power‑Up when:

- The feature is no longer needed (e.g., the project has ended).  
- You have switched to a different tool that offers the same capability.  
- The Power‑Up’s free tier limits are reached and you don’t wish to upgrade.

### How to Disable or Remove a Power‑Up

1. Click **Power‑Ups** in the board menu.  
2. Locate the Power‑Up you want to turn off.  
3. Click the **“...”** (more options) button next to it.  
4. Choose **“Disable”** to keep the Power‑Up listed but turned off, or **“Remove”** to delete it from the board entirely.  

Disabling is reversible—just re‑enable it later. Removing will require you to add the Power‑Up again if you change your mind.

### Monitoring Usage

Trello doesn’t provide built‑in analytics for Power‑Up usage, but you can gauge impact by:

- Observing board load times (if a board feels slower after adding several Power‑Ups).  
- Checking external service logs (e.g., Slack’s App Management page shows how many messages the Trello integration posted).  

If a Power‑Up appears idle for weeks, it may be a candidate for removal.

---

## Exploring the Full Power‑Up Ecosystem

### Categories to Explore

- **Productivity:** Calendar, Custom Fields, Card Repeater.  
- **Communication:** Slack, Microsoft Teams, Email.  
- **File Management:** Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive.  
- **Reporting & Analytics:** Burndown, Chart, Planyway.  
- **Automation:** Butler (covered in Chapter 7), Zapier (connects to thousands of apps).

### Free vs. Paid Power‑Ups

Many Power‑Ups offer a **free tier** that suffices for small teams or occasional use. Paid plans usually unlock:

- Higher usage limits (e.g., more than 10 automated Slack messages per month).  
- Advanced features (e.g., multi‑board syncing, premium support).  

The Power‑Up’s description page always lists pricing details, so you can compare before committing.

### Community‑Built vs. Official Power‑Ups

- **Official Power‑Ups** are built by the Trello team or its partners and receive regular updates.  
- **Community Power‑Ups** are created by third‑party developers. They can be very powerful (e.g., a GitHub integration), but they may have less reliable support.

When you try a community Power‑Up, check the user reviews and the last‑updated date to gauge its health.

---

## Real‑World Scenario: A Student Planning a Group Project

**Background:** Maya is leading a university capstone project with four teammates. She wants a single board to track tasks, share research documents, and keep everyone aware of upcoming meetings.

1. **Set up the board** (see Chapter 2). She creates three lists: *Ideas*, *In Progress*, *Done*.  
2. **Add the Calendar Power‑Up** so that every task with a due date appears on a shared calendar. She syncs the board with her Google Calendar, which automatically adds a **“Submit Draft”** reminder on the deadline date.  
3. **Enable the Google Drive Power‑Up**. Each teammate uploads their literature review to a shared Drive folder, then attaches the file directly to the relevant card. When Maya updates the bibliography, the attachment on the card reflects the latest version without re‑uploading.  
4. **Connect Slack** (the class uses a Slack channel called `#capstone‑updates`). The Slack Power‑Up is configured to post a message whenever a card moves to *Done*, giving the team a quick “progress” ping.  
5. **Configure permissions**: Maya, as board admin, grants her teammates “Comment” rights (already covered in Chapter 6) and lets only herself edit Power‑Up settings.  
6. **Mid‑semester review:** The team decides they no longer need the Slack notifications because they now meet weekly in person. Maya disables the Slack Power‑Up, keeping the Calendar and Google Drive integrations active.  
7. **Project wrap‑up:** After the final presentation, Maya removes the Calendar Power‑Up (no more deadlines) and leaves the Google Drive Power‑Up for archival reference.

Through this workflow, Maya demonstrates how adding, configuring, and later pruning Power‑Ups keeps the board lean yet powerful.

---

## Best Practices for Using Power‑Ups

- **Start small.** Add one Power‑Up, test it for a week, then decide if you need another.  
- **Align Power‑Ups with existing tools.** If your team already uses Google Drive, the Drive Power‑Up will feel natural; avoid adding a duplicate file‑storage Power‑Up.  
- **Limit board clutter.** Too many Power‑Ups can crowd the toolbar. Hide rarely used ones by disabling them.  
- **Review permissions regularly.** Ensure only trusted members can modify integration settings.  
- **Document your Power‑Ups.** Add a short note in a board description or a “Power‑Up Guide” card so new members understand what each integration does.  
- **Monitor costs.** Keep track of any subscription fees; many free tiers are sufficient for small projects.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Power‑Ups are plug‑ins** that connect Trello to other services or add new board features.  
- **The Power‑Up Directory** is the central place to discover, add, and manage integrations.  
- **Three starter Power‑Ups**—Calendar, Slack, and Google Drive—cover common needs: visualizing dates, staying in sync with communication tools, and handling files.  
- **Configuration steps** involve enabling the Power‑Up, authorizing external accounts, and setting board‑specific options (e.g., which Slack channel to post to).  
- **Disable or remove** Power‑Ups when they’re no longer useful to keep the board fast and tidy.  
- **Explore categories** (Productivity, Communication, etc.) and weigh free versus paid options before committing.  
- **Follow best practices**: add Power‑Ups gradually, align them with existing workflows, limit who can change settings, and document their purpose for the team.

By mastering Power‑Ups, you turn a simple Kanban board into a flexible hub that works hand‑in‑hand with the tools you already love. Happy integrating!

modules.title: Advanced Board Views: Calendar, Dashboard, and Timeline
modules.content:
## Switching Between Board, Calendar, and Timeline Views  

Imagine you’re coordinating a product launch that involves design, development, and marketing. The **Board view** gives you a classic Kanban layout—cards move from “Ideas” to “In Progress” to “Done.” But as the launch date approaches, you need to see *when* each task is due, and how the work fits together over weeks. That’s where the **Calendar** and **Timeline** views become indispensable.

### How to toggle views  

1. **Locate the view selector** – In the upper‑right corner of any board, click the **“Views”** icon (it looks like a grid).  
2. **Choose your view** – A dropdown lists the available options: **Board**, **Calendar**, and **Timeline**.  
3. **Remember your last choice** – Trello remembers the view you selected, so the next time you open the board it will open in the same mode.  

> **Tip:** You can keep the Board view open in one browser tab while exploring Calendar or Timeline in another tab. This makes side‑by‑side comparison easy for multi‑stakeholder meetings.

## Using the Calendar View Effectively  

The Calendar view turns every card’s **due date** into a visual event on a monthly grid. It’s the fastest way to answer the question, “What’s due when?”

### Setting up cards for the Calendar  

- **Add a due date** – Open a card, click the **Due Date** field, and pick a date (and optionally a time). The card instantly appears on the Calendar.  
- **Use reminders** – If you enabled reminders in earlier chapters, they still fire, but now you also see the upcoming reminder as a shaded bar on the calendar.  

### Navigating the Calendar  

| Action | How to do it |
|--------|--------------|
| **Switch months** | Click the left/right arrows at the top of the calendar, or use ⟨ ← ⟩ / ⟨ → ⟩ keyboard shortcuts. |
| **Toggle weeks** | Click the **“Week”** button to zoom in; click **“Month”** to zoom out. |
| **Drag‑and‑drop** | Grab a card on the calendar and drop it on a new date to reschedule. Trello updates the card’s due date automatically. |
| **Show/hide weekends** | Click the gear icon → **Settings** → toggle **“Show weekends”**. This cleans up the view for teams that only work weekdays. |

### Filtering within the Calendar  

1. Click the **Filter** button (the funnel icon) in the Calendar toolbar.  
2. Choose one or more of the following criteria:  

   - **Labels** – e.g., only “Marketing” cards.  
   - **Members** – e.g., tasks assigned to *Alex*.  
   - **Due date range** – e.g., “Next 14 days”.  

3. The calendar instantly redraws, showing only the matching cards.  

> **Scenario:** Your marketing lead wants to see only the campaigns scheduled for the next two weeks. They filter by the “Marketing” label and the “Next 14 days” date range, giving a clean, focused view.

## Getting Insight with the Dashboard Power‑Up  

Visual reports turn raw card data into charts you can share in meetings or embed in presentations. The **Dashboard Power‑Up** is Trello’s native analytics add‑on; it does not require a third‑party subscription.

### Enabling the Dashboard Power‑Up  

1. Open the **Power‑Ups** menu (refer to Chapter 8).  
2. Search for **“Dashboard”** and click **Add**.  
3. The Dashboard appears as a new tab on your board, alongside Board, Calendar, and Timeline.  

### Building a useful dashboard  

When you first open the Dashboard, you’ll see a set of **widgets**—small visual components you can add, move, or remove. Common widgets for a launch board include:

- **Cards by List** – a bar chart showing how many cards sit in each list (e.g., “Design”, “Development”, “QA”).  
- **Cards by Label** – a pie chart that breaks down work by label (e.g., “Feature”, “Bug”, “Marketing”).  
- **Cards by Due Date** – a line chart that visualizes upcoming workload over the next 30 days.  
- **Burn‑up Chart** – useful for Agile teams; tracks completed versus total work over time.  

To add a widget: click **“Add Widget”**, select the type, then configure the filter (e.g., only cards with the “Sprint 1” label).  

### Interpreting the dashboard  

- **High‑density bars** in “Cards by List” indicate bottlenecks—perhaps “Development” has too many cards waiting.  
- **Large slices** in “Cards by Label” reveal where effort is concentrated—maybe “Bug” takes up 40 % of the board, prompting a quality‑focus meeting.  
- **Burn‑up trends** that plateau suggest the team may need extra resources or scope adjustment.  

### Exporting and sharing  

- Click the **Export** icon on the Dashboard tab to download a CSV file of the underlying data.  
- Use the **Share** button to generate a public link (read‑only) that you can embed in Slack or email.  

## Filtering Cards Across All Views  

Filters are a universal way to narrow focus, no matter whether you’re looking at the Board, Calendar, or Timeline.

### The filter toolbar  

- **Location** – The funnel icon appears in the top‑right of each view.  
- **Options** – You can filter by **due date**, **label**, **member**, and **keyword** (searches titles and descriptions).  

### Step‑by‑step filtering  

1. Click the funnel icon.  
2. Tick the checkboxes for the labels you want (e.g., “Design”).  
3. Choose a member from the dropdown (e.g., “Maria”).  
4. Optionally set a date range (e.g., “Due in the next 7 days”).  
5. Press **Apply** – All three views instantly reflect the filtered set.  

### Saving filter presets (workaround)  

Trello does not yet support permanent filter presets, but you can **bookmark** a URL that includes filter parameters. After applying a filter, copy the URL from the address bar; reopening that link restores the same filter state.  

> **Example:** The project manager creates a bookmark called “Marketing‑Week‑View” that always shows only “Marketing” cards due this week. Team members can click the bookmark to jump straight to that filtered view.

## Customizing Views for Different Team Roles or Project Phases  

One board often serves multiple audiences—designers, developers, marketers, and executives—each of whom needs a tailored visual experience.

### Role‑based view defaults  

1. **Create a view‑specific shortcut** – In the **Views** dropdown, hover over a view (e.g., Timeline) and click the **pin** icon. This pins the view as a quick‑access button for anyone who opens the board.  
2. **Communicate defaults** – In the board description or a pinned card, note which view each role should start with (e.g., “Developers: open in Timeline”).  

### Phase‑specific customizations  

| Project Phase | Recommended Primary View | Typical Filters |
|---------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| **Planning** | Board (to map ideas) | No filter or “Label = Idea” |
| **Scheduling** | Calendar (to set dates) | “Due in next 30 days” |
| **Execution** | Timeline (to see overlaps) | “Label = Sprint 1” + “Member = *” |
| **Review** | Dashboard (to assess metrics) | “Cards by List” + “Burn‑up” |

### Practical walk‑through  

*Scenario:* Your product launch board moves from the **Planning** phase to **Execution**.  

1. **Switch to Timeline view** – Click the Timeline tab.  
2. **Apply a filter** – Filter by the label “Sprint 2”. The Timeline now shows only the cards that belong to the current sprint, with bars indicating start and due dates.  
3. **Save the filtered view** – Copy the URL (which now includes the filter query) and add it to a card named “Sprint 2 Timeline”. Team members click that card to open the filtered Timeline instantly.  

### Advanced tip: Syncing with external calendars  

If your organization uses Google Calendar or Outlook, you can **export** the Calendar view as an iCal feed:  

1. Open Calendar view.  
2. Click the **gear** → **Export Calendar** → **iCal URL**.  
3. Paste the URL into your external calendar’s “Subscribe to calendar” field.  

Now every due date on Trello appears as an event in your personal calendar, keeping you in sync even when you’re away from Trello.

## Tips & Tricks for Mastery  

- **Keyboard shortcuts** – Press **‘B’** to open the view selector, **‘C’** for Calendar, **‘T’** for Timeline.  
- **Quick date changes** – Hover over a card’s due date on the Board view and click the pencil icon to edit without opening the full card.  
- **Multi‑Power‑Up synergy** – Combine the **Calendar Power‑Up** (if you prefer a separate calendar pane) with the native Calendar view for richer filtering options.  
- **Color‑code labels for visual scanning** – Consistent label colors across views make it easier to spot categories at a glance.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Switching views** is as simple as using the view selector; each view serves a distinct purpose—Board for workflow, Calendar for due dates, Timeline for schedule overlap.  
- **Calendar view** lets you see all due dates on a monthly grid, drag‑and‑drop to reschedule, and filter by label, member, or date range.  
- **Dashboard Power‑Up** provides visual reports (charts, burn‑up) that turn card data into actionable insights; enable it from the Power‑Ups menu.  
- **Filters** work consistently across all views, allowing you to focus on specific due dates, labels, or team members; bookmark filtered URLs for quick reuse.  
- **Customizing views** for different roles or project phases improves clarity—designers may prefer Board, developers Timeline, marketers Calendar, and executives Dashboard.  
- **Syncing** the Calendar view with external calendars and using shortcuts keeps your schedule visible wherever you work.  

By mastering these advanced views, you transform a static Kanban board into a dynamic, role‑aware planning hub that keeps every team member aligned and every deadline in sight.

modules.title: Organizing Large Projects: Using Multi-Boards and Templates
modules.content:
## Why Multi‑Board Projects Matter  

Imagine you’re launching a new smartphone. The effort involves three distinct teams: **Marketing**, **Engineering**, and **Customer Support**. Each team needs its own workflow—campaign planning, sprint tracking, and issue triage—yet the project’s success depends on how well these workflows stay aligned. Trying to jam all of that into a single board quickly becomes chaotic: lists overflow, cards get lost, and stakeholders can’t see the pieces that matter to them.  

Using **multiple boards** lets each team work in a space that matches its language and cadence, while **templates** and **board links** keep the whole effort synchronized. This chapter shows you how to set up that structure from scratch, reuse it for future launches, and keep your Trello workspace tidy.

---

## Building a Reusable Project Template  

A **Board Template** is a ready‑made skeleton you can copy whenever a similar project starts. Think of it as a “master copy” that contains the essential Lists, boilerplate Cards, and any Power‑Ups you want to carry over.

### 1. Sketch the Core Stages  

1. **Identify the universal phases** of the project type.  
   - For a product launch: `Planning → Design → Development → QA → Release → Post‑Launch`.  
2. **Create a List for each phase** on a new board.  
   - Because you already know how to add Lists (see Chapter 3), simply click **Add another list** and name it accordingly.  

### 2. Add Boilerplate Cards  

Boilerplate cards are the “starter tasks” that appear on every new board of this type.  

- **Example Card:** *Kick‑off meeting* (placed in the `Planning` list).  
- **Checklist:** Add a checklist named **Launch Checklist** with items like “Define target audience”, “Set launch date”, “Prepare press kit”.  

Using **Checklists**, **Due dates**, and **Labels** (introduced earlier) on these cards gives every copy a consistent baseline.

### 3. Turn the Board into a Template  

1. Open the board’s **Menu** (right‑hand side).  
2. Select **More** → **Settings** → **Convert to Template**.  
3. Confirm the conversion.  

The board now displays a **Template** badge. Whenever you need a new launch board, you’ll start from this exact layout, saving hours of setup.

---

## Duplicating a Board for a New Project  

When a fresh project kicks off—say, the next smartphone model—you don’t have to rebuild the board manually. You **duplicate** (or **copy**) the template.

### Using the “Copy Board” Feature  

1. From the **Home** view, locate the template board.  
2. Click the three‑dot **⋯** menu on the board thumbnail.  
3. Choose **Copy Board**.  
4. In the dialog, give the new board a specific name (e.g., *Galaxy X Launch – Q4 2026*).  
5. Decide whether to copy **Cards**, **Lists**, **Board Settings**, and **Power‑Ups**. For a template, you’ll usually keep everything except the **attachments** that are project‑specific.  

### What Gets Copied vs. What Stays Unique  

| Copied | Remains Unique |
|--------|----------------|
| Lists and their order | Board background & cover image (you can change later) |
| Boilerplate cards (with checklists, labels) | Card members, due dates, comments (they’re cleared on copy) |
| Enabled Power‑Ups | Board members (you’ll add the current team) |

By default, Trello strips out members, comments, and due dates, giving you a clean slate while preserving the structure you need.

---

## Connecting Boards for Cross‑Project Visibility  

Even though each team works on its own board, they often need to see each other’s progress. Trello offers two straightforward ways to link boards: **card linking** and the **Board Link Power‑Up**.

### Linking Cards Across Boards  

1. Open a card on the **Marketing** board that represents the “Launch Campaign”.  
2. In the **Add to card** field, type `@` followed by the name of the board you want to reference (e.g., `@Engineering`).  
3. Select the target board, then choose the specific card (e.g., “Beta Firmware Ready”).  

The original card now shows a **linked card** section at the bottom, providing a clickable shortcut to the related item on the other board. This method works without any additional Power‑Ups.

### Using the Board Link Power‑Up  

If you prefer a visual pane that lists related boards:

1. Open the board’s **Menu** → **Power‑Ups**.  
2. Search for **Board Links** (a native Power‑Up) and click **Add**.  
3. Click **Add Link** on the board, give it a label like “Engineering Board”, and select the board to connect.  

The linked board appears as a card on the current board, making it easy for anyone to hop between contexts.

### Example: Marketing ↔ Design ↔ Support  

- **Marketing Card:** “Press Release Draft” links to the **Design** board’s card “Product Images”.  
- **Support Card:** “FAQ Draft” links to the **Marketing** board’s card “Launch Date Announcement”.  

Whenever a linked card is moved to a new List, the reference updates automatically, keeping every stakeholder in the loop.

---

## Navigating Quickly with the Home Dashboard  

When you manage dozens of boards, finding the right one at a glance is crucial. Trello’s **Home** view is the central hub for board navigation.

### The Home Layout  

- **Recent Boards** – shows the boards you’ve visited in the last 30 days.  
- **Starred Boards** – boards you’ve **starred** for fast access (click the star icon on any board).  
- **Team Sections** – groups boards by the team you belong to.  

Because you already know how to **star** a board (click the star next to its name), you can create a personal “quick‑launch” area for all your active project boards.

### Pinning Favorite Boards  

1. Open the board you use most (e.g., *Current Sprint*).  
2. Click the star icon at the top of the board.  
3. The board now appears at the top of the **Starred Boards** list on Home.  

You can star as many boards as you like; Home will automatically sort them by most‑recent activity.

### Using Filters and Search  

- **Search bar** (top‑right) lets you type a board name, label, or card title.  
- **Filters** (click the funnel icon) let you narrow results by **Team**, **Board Visibility** (private, team‑visible, public), or **Labels**.  

These tools become indispensable when you have multiple launch boards across several product lines.

---

## Keeping the Workspace Clean: Archiving Completed Boards  

A cluttered board list makes it harder to locate active projects. Trello distinguishes between **archiving** (soft delete) and **deleting** (permanent removal). For most workflows, you’ll **archive** completed boards.

### Archive vs. Delete  

- **Archive** – moves the board to the **Archived Boards** section; you can restore it later.  
- **Delete** – permanently erases the board and all its data; recovery is impossible.  

Because you may need to reference a past launch for reporting, archiving is the safer default.

### Bulk Archiving Steps  

1. From **Home**, click **Boards** → **View All Boards**.  
2. Click the **Filter** icon and select **Closed Boards** to see already archived items.  
3. To archive a board: open the board, go to **Menu** → **More** → **Close Board**.  
4. Confirm the action. The board disappears from your active list and appears under **Closed Boards**.  

If you have many finished boards, repeat the process or use a **Butler** rule (covered in Chapter 7) to automatically close a board when its last card is moved to a “Done” list.

### Restoring an Archived Board  

1. In **Home**, click **Boards** → **Closed Boards**.  
2. Locate the board you want to bring back.  
3. Click **Reopen**.  

The board returns to its original position, preserving all Lists and Cards exactly as they were when closed.

---

## Tips for Scaling Multi‑Board Workflows  

Even with templates and links, large programs can become unwieldy. The following habits make the system sustainable.

- **Naming Conventions** – start every board with a consistent prefix, e.g., `Launch – <Product> – <Quarter>`. This makes searching and sorting easier.  
- **Cross‑Board Labels** – create a set of standard Labels (e.g., **Urgent**, **Blocked**, **Milestone**) and apply them across all boards. When you filter by a label on Home, you’ll see every card sharing that status, regardless of board.  
- **Butler Automation** – set up a simple rule: *When a board is copied from a template, add the “New Project” label to all cards in the first list.* This keeps the new board’s tasks highlighted without manual effort.  
- **Regular Clean‑Up Cadence** – schedule a monthly review to archive boards that have been closed for more than 30 days.  

By embedding these practices early, you’ll avoid the “board sprawl” that plagues many growing teams.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Board Templates** let you capture a repeatable project skeleton—including Lists, boilerplate Cards, and Power‑Ups—so you can spin up new projects in minutes.  
- **Copying a board** from a template preserves structure while clearing out members, comments, and due dates, giving you a clean starting point.  
- **Linking cards** or using the **Board Links Power‑Up** creates live connections between related boards, enabling cross‑team visibility without duplicating information.  
- The **Home dashboard** centralizes navigation; starring, filtering, and searching let you jump to any active board instantly.  
- **Archiving** finished boards (instead of deleting) keeps your workspace tidy while preserving history for future reference; you can restore them anytime.  

With these tools, you can confidently scale Trello from single‑board tasks to full‑fledged, multi‑board projects—maintaining clarity, speed, and control every step of the way.

modules.title: Mobile App Basics: Managing Trello on the Go
modules.content:
## A Day in the Life: Fixing a Project Bottleneck While Waiting for Your Coffee

You’re standing in line at the coffee shop, phone in hand, and a teammate just messaged you: *“The design mock‑up is stuck on the “Review” list—can you add a comment?”* You glance at your laptop a few minutes later, but the meeting is about to start. With the Trello mobile app open, you tap a few times, add a comment, attach a quick photo of the latest sketch, and move the card to “In Progress”—all before the barista hands you your latte.  

That split‑second ability to edit boards, respond to updates, and capture fresh content is what the mobile app brings to a digital Kanban board. In the sections that follow, you’ll learn how to get the app onto your device, keep it in perfect sync with your desktop boards, and use its core features to stay productive wherever you are.

---

## Download and Install the Trello Mobile App

### iOS (iPhone & iPad)

1. **Open the App Store** – the blue icon with a white “A”.
2. **Search for “Trello”** – the official app is published by *Atlassian* and shows the familiar board icon.
3. **Tap “Get” → “Install”** – you may need to confirm with Face ID, Touch ID, or your Apple ID password.
4. **Launch the app** – it will appear on your home screen once installation finishes.

> **Tip:** If you have an iPad, you can choose the “iPhone‑only” version or the “iPad‑optimized” version. The latter shows more of the board at once, which can be handy for larger screens.

### Android (Phones & Tablets)

1. **Open Google Play Store** – the multicolored triangle icon.
2. **Search for “Trello”** – again, look for the Atlassian publisher.
3. **Tap “Install”** – the download begins automatically.
4. **Open the app** – you’ll find it in your app drawer or on the home screen.

> **Tip:** Android devices vary widely in screen size. If you have a tablet, you can enable “tablet mode” in the app’s settings for a broader view of your board.

### First‑time Sign‑In

- Use the same **email address** and **password** you employ on the desktop version.  
- If you employ **single‑sign‑on (SSO)** through your organization, tap the “Sign in with Google/Office 365” button and follow the corporate login flow.  
- **Two‑factor authentication (2FA)** works the same way as on the web; you’ll receive a code via your chosen method.

Once signed in, the app automatically pulls in every board you have access to—private, team‑visible, or public—so you’re ready to work immediately.

---

## Getting Started: First Launch and Sync

### Automatic Synchronization

Trello’s mobile client uses **real‑time sync**. Any change you make on your phone—adding a card, moving a list, editing a comment—appears within seconds on the desktop version, and vice‑versa. The sync works over Wi‑Fi or cellular data, depending on your connection settings.

#### Controlling Sync Settings

1. Open the **hamburger menu** (three horizontal lines) in the top‑left corner.  
2. Tap **Settings → Sync**.  
3. Choose one of the following:
   - **Automatic** – the default; updates happen instantly.
   - **Wi‑Fi only** – conserves cellular data; updates only when connected to Wi‑Fi.
   - **Manual** – you decide when to pull changes by pulling down on the board view.

### Verifying Sync

- **Pull‑to‑refresh**: Swipe down on any board screen to force a sync.  
- **Sync indicator**: A small rotating arrow appears at the top of the screen while the app communicates with Trello’s servers.  

If you ever see a **“Sync error”** banner, tap it to retry or check your internet connection.

---

## Navigating the Mobile Interface

The mobile layout condenses the desktop experience into a series of touch‑friendly panels.

| Element | Desktop Equivalent | Mobile Interaction |
|---------|--------------------|--------------------|
| **Boards list** | Sidebar showing all boards | Swipe right from the left edge or tap the hamburger menu |
| **Board view** | Full‑screen board with lists | Pinch‑to‑zoom, swipe left/right to scroll horizontally |
| **List column** | Vertical column of cards | Tap a list header to collapse/expand it |
| **Card** | Individual task | Tap to open full details; long‑press for quick actions |
| **Quick add (+) button** | “Add a card” field at the bottom of a list | Tap the **+** floating button at the bottom right of the screen |
| **Search** | Top‑right search bar | Pull down on the boards list, then type in the search field |

### Bottom Navigation Bar

1. **Home** – Returns you to the boards list.  
2. **Notifications** – Shows recent mentions, due‑date alerts, and board activity.  
3. **Add** – Opens a contextual menu for creating a board, list, or card.  
4. **Search** – Lets you find cards, members, or boards quickly.  
5. **Profile** – Access your account settings, logged‑in devices, and logout option.

> **Pro tip:** Swipe left on a board in the boards list to reveal **Archive** and **Delete** shortcuts—useful for cleaning up old projects without navigating into each board.

---

## Creating and Managing Cards on the Go

### Adding a New Card

1. Open the target board and locate the list where the card belongs.  
2. Tap the **+** floating button → **Add Card**.  
3. Type the **title** (the primary piece of information a card holds).  
4. (Optional) Tap **Add description** to enter more detail.  
5. Tap **Create**.  

The new card appears at the bottom of the list, just as on the desktop.

### Editing Card Details

- **Open a card** by tapping it.  
- At the top, you’ll see the **title**; tap the pencil icon to edit.  
- Below, you can add or modify:
  - **Checklists** – tap **Add checklist**, name it, then add items.  
  - **Due dates** – tap the calendar icon, select a date, optionally set a time.  
  - **Labels** – tap the label icon, choose existing colors, or create a new one.  
  - **Attachments** – see the next section for media capture.  
  - **Comments** – type at the bottom and tap **Send**.

All edits are saved instantly and reflected on any other device you’re logged into.

### Moving Cards Between Lists

#### Drag‑and‑Drop (Touch)

1. Open the board view.  
2. **Press and hold** the card you want to move until it lifts.  
3. **Drag** it left or right to the target list.  
4. **Release** to drop the card.

#### Quick Move (Tap)

1. Open the card.  
2. Tap the **Move** icon (two arrows).  
3. Select the destination board and list from the dropdown menus.  
4. Confirm by tapping **Move**.

Both methods update the card’s location instantly.

### Archiving vs. Deleting

- **Archive** removes the card from view but keeps it searchable and restorable.  
- **Delete** permanently erases the card; this option appears only after archiving.  

To archive a card from the mobile view, open the card, tap the three‑dot menu (⋮), and choose **Archive**.

---

## Staying Informed: Notifications and Updates

### Types of Notifications

- **Mentions** – When someone uses `@yourname` in a comment.  
- **Due‑date alerts** – Pushes when a card’s deadline approaches.  
- **Board activity** – New cards, moved cards, or added comments.  

All notification types were introduced earlier; the mobile app simply surfaces them in a compact feed.

### Configuring Notification Preferences

1. Open **Settings** via the hamburger menu.  
2. Tap **Notifications**.  
3. Choose between:
   - **All activity** – Every change across all boards.  
   - **Mentions only** – Only when you’re directly addressed.  
   - **Custom** – Pick specific boards or members to follow.  

You can also toggle **Push notifications** (alerts that appear even when the app is closed) and **Email notifications**.

### Responding to a Notification

- Tap the notification in the **Notifications** tab.  
- The app opens the relevant card or board, placing you directly where the action occurred.  
- From there, you can comment, add a label, or move the card—no need to navigate manually.

> **Scenario:** While commuting, you receive a push notification that a due date is tomorrow. Tapping it opens the card, where you quickly add a **“High Priority”** label and check the checklist to ensure nothing is missed.

---

## Capturing Media: Photos and Voice Notes Directly Into Cards

One of the mobile app’s biggest advantages is the ability to attach fresh content without leaving the app.

### Adding a Photo

1. Open the target card.  
2. Tap the **Attachment** (paper‑clip) icon.  
3. Choose **Camera** to take a new picture, or **Gallery** to pick an existing image.  
4. After confirming, the photo appears as an attachment thumbnail.  

You can add a **caption** by tapping the photo’s name field, which is helpful for context (e.g., “Whiteboard sketch from today’s stand‑up”).

### Recording a Voice Note

1. Inside the card, tap the **Attachment** icon.  
2. Select **Voice note** (microphone symbol).  
3. Press **Record**, speak, then press **Stop**.  
4. Tap **Save**; the audio file appears as an attachment.  

Team members can play the voice note directly from the card, making it ideal for quick explanations or meeting recaps.

### Using Attachments in Comments

If you prefer to keep the card’s main description clean, you can **embed** a photo or voice note in a comment:

- After attaching the media, tap **Add comment**.  
- The attachment will be listed beneath the comment field; you can type a brief note and then **Send**.

All attachments sync across devices, so a photo taken on your phone will be viewable on the desktop version instantly.

---

## Working Offline: What Happens When You Lose Connectivity?

The mobile app caches board data locally, allowing you to continue working even without an internet connection.

1. **Create or edit cards** while offline.  
2. The app marks these changes with a small **cloud with a slash** icon.  
3. Once you regain connectivity, the app automatically syncs the pending changes.  

If a conflict arises—e.g., the same card was edited on another device while you were offline—the app will prompt you to **keep your version**, **accept the server version**, or **merge** the two manually.

> **Pro tip:** To avoid data loss, try to connect to Wi‑Fi before making large batches of edits, especially when adding many attachments.

---

## Tips for Maximizing Mobile Productivity

- **Pin frequently used boards**: In the boards list, swipe left on a board and tap the pin icon. Pinned boards appear at the top for quick access.  
- **Use widgets (iOS/Android)**: Add a Trello widget to your home screen that shows a single board’s lists, letting you glance at tasks without opening the app.  
- **Leverage quick actions**: Long‑press a card in the board view to bring up a context menu with shortcuts for **Copy**, **Move**, **Archive**, and **Add label**.  
- **Set custom board backgrounds**: A familiar visual cue (e.g., a project’s logo) can help you locate the right board faster on a small screen.  

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Install** the Trello app from the App Store or Google Play, then sign in with the same credentials you use on the desktop.  
- **Sync** happens automatically; you can adjust settings to limit data usage or force a manual refresh.  
- The **mobile interface** mirrors desktop concepts—boards, lists, cards—through touch‑friendly gestures (tap, swipe, drag‑and‑drop).  
- **Create, edit, and move cards** directly from your phone or tablet, using either drag‑and‑drop or the quick‑move dialog.  
- **Stay on top of activity** via the built‑in notifications feed, customizing which alerts you receive.  
- **Capture fresh media**—photos, voice notes, and other attachments—without leaving the app, and they sync instantly to all devices.  
- **Offline mode** lets you keep working when the network drops, queuing changes for later synchronization.  

With these tools in hand, your Trello board is no longer tied to a desk. Whether you’re waiting for a coffee, commuting, or on a construction site, you can keep your workflow visible, collaborative, and up‑to‑date—all from the palm of your hand.

modules.title: Best Practices for Trello Organization: Tips from the Pros
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Imagine Maya, a freelance graphic designer who juggles client work, personal projects, and a side hustle selling prints online. She started with a single Trello **Board** for each client, but over months the boards multiplied: “Client A – Design,” “Client A – Feedback,” “Print Shop,” “Ideas,” “Marketing,” and a catch‑all “Stuff To Do.” When Maya opens Trello, she sees a sprawling list of boards, each brimming with cards, labels, and a handful of **Power‑Ups** she tried once and forgot about. She spends more time searching for the right board than actually designing.

Maya’s story is common. The good news? A handful of proven habits—what the pros call “clean board” strategies—can turn that chaos into a clear, focused workspace. The following sections walk you through each habit, showing how to apply it step‑by‑step, even if you’re just starting out.

---

## 1. Embrace the “One Board, One Purpose” Rule  

### Why a Single Purpose Matters  

A **Board** is a digital canvas that makes work visible. When a board tries to serve several unrelated purposes, the visual hierarchy collapses: cards from different projects compete for attention, filters become noisy, and the board’s original intent gets lost. Keeping each board dedicated to a single purpose restores the clarity that makes Kanban so powerful.

### How to Identify a Board’s Core Purpose  

1. **Write a one‑sentence mission** for the board.  
   *Example:* “Track all tasks for the ‘Spring Launch’ marketing campaign.”  
2. **List the types of work** the board should contain. If anything falls outside that list, it belongs elsewhere.  
3. **Ask yourself:** “If I had to delete this board tomorrow, what would I lose?” If the answer is vague, the board is probably too broad.

### Auditing Your Existing Boards  

1. **Gather all boards** on the Trello home screen.  
2. **For each board**, read its mission statement (add one if missing).  
3. **Group boards** that share the same purpose.  
4. **Consolidate or split**:  
   * If two boards serve the same purpose, merge them.  
   * If one board covers multiple purposes, create separate boards and move the relevant cards.  

### Quick Checklist  

- ✅ Each board has a clear, written purpose.  
- ✅ No board mixes unrelated projects or workflows.  
- ✅ Boards are named to reflect their purpose (e.g., “Blog Content Calendar”).  

---

## 2. Use Labels Consistently for Instant Visual Filtering  

### The Power of a Well‑Defined Label System  

Labels are the colored tags you already know from earlier chapters. When used consistently, they become a glance‑readable map of priority, department, or status—no need to open each card.

### Building a Simple Label Scheme  

| Color | Suggested Use | Example Name |
|-------|---------------|--------------|
| Red   | **Urgent / High Priority** | “Urgent” |
| Orange| **Waiting / Blocked** | “On Hold” |
| Yellow| **Ideas / To Explore** | “Idea” |
| Green | **Completed / Done** | “Done” |
| Blue  | **Team / Department** | “Design” |
| Purple| **Client / Category** | “Client A” |

**Tip:** Start with **three** core colors (e.g., priority, status, team) and expand only when you truly need more distinction.

### Applying Labels Without Overwhelm  

1. **Create a label cheat‑sheet** in the board description or a dedicated “Reference” card.  
2. **Assign labels at card creation** (you can set default labels in the board settings).  
3. **Use the filter bar** (top right) to toggle one or more labels and instantly view a focused slice of work.  

### Consistency Checklist  

- ✅ Labels are limited to a manageable set (no more than 6–8 per board).  
- ✅ Each label has a clear, documented meaning.  
- ✅ Team members understand and use the same label conventions.  

---

## 3. Keep Active Lists to 5‑7 for Maximum Focus  

### Why Fewer Lists Work Better  

Lists represent workflow stages or time‑based categories. When you exceed 7 active lists, the board’s vertical space becomes crowded, and it’s harder to spot bottlenecks. A lean list structure also aligns with the classic Kanban principle of limiting work‑in‑progress (WIP).

### Designing a Streamlined List Layout  

A typical “one‑purpose” board might follow this pattern:

1. **Backlog** – ideas not yet scheduled  
2. **To Do** – tasks ready to start  
3. **In Progress** – work currently underway  
4. **Review** – awaiting feedback or approval  
5. **Done** – completed items  

If you need extra granularity (e.g., “Waiting for Client”), consider **sub‑lists** via **Checklists** inside a card, or use **labels** instead of an additional list.

### Managing Overflow  

- **Archive finished lists**: Click the list’s menu → “Archive List.”  
- **Create a “Future” list** for items that will become active later; keep it minimal.  
- **Use the “Search” function** to locate cards that belong elsewhere rather than adding a new list.  

### List‑Limit Checklist  

- ✅ No more than 7 active lists are visible at any time.  
- ✅ Each list has a clear purpose that aligns with the board’s mission.  
- ✅ Overflow or completed lists are archived regularly.  

---

## 4. Schedule Regular Board Cleanups  

### The 15‑Minute Weekly Reset  

A board that is tidy today can become messy tomorrow. Setting a recurring **weekly cleanup** habit (e.g., every Friday at 4 pm) prevents clutter from snowballing.

### Weekly Cleanup Routine  

1. **Review “To Do” and “In Progress”**: Move any stale cards to the appropriate list or archive them if they’re no longer relevant.  
2. **Archive completed cards**: Use the board menu → “Archive All Cards” in the “Done” list.  
3. **Check labels**: Remove any that are no longer used; update the cheat‑sheet.  
4. **Evaluate Power‑Ups**: Disable any you haven’t used in the past month.  
5. **Rename or reorder lists** if the workflow has changed.  

### Automating the Cleanup (Optional)  

If you’re comfortable with **Butler**, you can create a rule such as:  
> “Every Sunday at 6 am, move cards in ‘Done’ that are older than 7 days to the archive.”

Even a simple manual routine, however, yields huge productivity gains.

### Cleanup Checklist  

- ✅ Stale cards have been moved or archived.  
- ✅ Unused labels are removed.  
- ✅ Power‑Ups are reviewed and trimmed.  
- ✅ Lists reflect the current workflow.  

---

## 5. Avoid Over‑Customizing with Too Many Power‑Ups  

### The Temptation of “Shiny New Features”  

Power‑Ups extend Trello with third‑party integrations (e.g., Calendar, Google Drive). While they can be game‑changing, each added Power‑Up consumes system resources and adds visual noise. The pros recommend **capping Power‑Ups at three per board**—enough to get the most value without overwhelming the interface.

### Choosing the Right Power‑Ups  

1. **Identify a concrete need** (e.g., “I need to see due dates on a calendar”).  
2. **Search the Power‑Ups directory** for the simplest tool that meets that need.  
3. **Enable it** and test for a week. If it doesn’t become part of your workflow, disable it.  

### Commonly Recommended Power‑Ups  

| Need | Recommended Power‑Up |
|------|----------------------|
| Calendar view of due dates | **Calendar** |
| Visualizing metrics | **Dashboard** |
| Connecting to a file repository | **Google Drive** (or **OneDrive**) |
| Automating repetitive actions | **Butler** (already covered) |

### Managing Power‑Ups  

- **Turn off unused Power‑Ups**: Board menu → “Power‑Ups” → “Disable.”  
- **Document active Power‑Ups** in a “Board Settings” card for team reference.  

### Power‑Up Checklist  

- ✅ No more than three Power‑Ups are active on any board.  
- ✅ Each Power‑Up solves a specific, recurring need.  
- ✅ Unused Power‑Ups are disabled and documented.  

---

## 6. Putting It All Together: A Sample Clean Board  

Below is a snapshot of a board that follows every best practice discussed. Feel free to replicate the structure in your own Trello workspace.

| **Board Name** | **Purpose** |
|----------------|------------|
| “Spring Launch – Marketing” | Track all tasks needed to launch the spring product line. |

### Lists (5 Active)  

1. **Backlog** – ideas and postponed tasks.  
2. **To Do** – tasks ready to start this week.  
3. **In Progress** – work currently being done.  
4. **Review** – awaiting stakeholder feedback.  
5. **Done** – completed tasks (archived weekly).  

### Labels (6 Consistent Colors)  

- **Red – Urgent**  
- **Orange – On Hold**  
- **Yellow – Idea**  
- **Green – Completed** (automatically applied by Butler when a card is moved to “Done”)  
- **Blue – Design Team**  
- **Purple – Client A**  

### Power‑Ups (3 Active)  

- **Calendar** – visual due‑date overview.  
- **Google Drive** – quick attachment of assets.  
- **Butler** – weekly cleanup automation (moves “Done” cards older than 7 days to archive).  

### Weekly Cleanup Routine (Friday, 4 pm)  

- Move any “In Progress” cards stuck > 3 days to “On Hold” (using the orange label).  
- Archive the “Done” list.  
- Review label usage and remove any that haven’t been applied in the past month.  
- Confirm that Calendar and Google Drive integrations are still needed.  

By following this template, Maya could replace her tangled web of boards with a single, purpose‑driven board that stays tidy, visual, and easy to navigate.

---

## 7. Quick Tips for Ongoing Success  

- **Name boards descriptively**: Include the project name and its purpose (e.g., “Q3 Budget – Finance”).  
- **Leverage the board description**: Summarize the purpose, label meanings, and cleanup schedule in one place.  
- **Use card templates** for recurring tasks (e.g., weekly reports) to keep label and checklist consistency.  
- **Limit guest access** to only the boards that match their role; unnecessary access adds noise.  
- **Celebrate a clean board**: When a weekly cleanup is complete, add a “✅ Cleaned” checklist item to a “Board Maintenance” card. Small wins reinforce the habit.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **One board, one purpose** keeps focus sharp and prevents cross‑project confusion.  
- **Consistent labels** act as instant visual filters; limit the set and document meanings.  
- **5‑7 active lists** provide a manageable workflow view; archive excess lists regularly.  
- **Weekly cleanups** (15 minutes) maintain a lean board—move, archive, and review.  
- **Power‑Ups** should be limited to the essentials (max three per board) to avoid overload.  

Adopting these habits transforms Trello from a simple task list into a disciplined, high‑visibility system that supports your productivity—just like the pros do. Happy organizing!

modules.title: Troubleshooting Common Trello Issues
modules.content:
## A Day in the Life of a Stressed Project Lead  

Emma is managing a product launch on Trello. She checks her **desktop board** at 9 am, adds a few new cards, and assigns teammates. By lunch, she pulls out her phone to update the status while on a client call. When she opens the **mobile app**, the new cards are nowhere to be found. Later, a teammate reports that a critical checklist is missing, and a Power‑Up that automatically moves cards based on due dates throws an error. Panic rises: *“Did I lose work? Can I get the board back?”*  

If you’ve ever felt like Emma, you’re not alone. The most common hiccups in Trello—sync gaps, vanished cards, misbehaving Power‑Ups, permission glitches, and accidental deletions—can all be resolved with a few systematic steps. Below you’ll learn how to diagnose and fix each problem, so you can get back to making work visible without missing a beat.

---

## 1. Sync Issues Between Desktop and Mobile Apps  

### Why Sync Can Fail  
Even though Trello stores everything in the cloud, the desktop web client and the mobile app maintain **local caches** to speed up loading. If the cache becomes outdated or the device loses internet connectivity, the two views can drift apart.

### Quick Diagnostic Checklist  

1. **Check Internet Connection** – Verify that both devices are online. A weak Wi‑Fi signal or cellular dropout often causes partial sync.  
2. **Refresh the Board** –  
   * Desktop: Click the **Refresh** button (or press `F5`).  
   * Mobile: Pull down from the top of the board view to trigger a manual sync.  
3. **Confirm Account Consistency** – Ensure you’re signed into the same Trello account on both devices.  
4. **Look for Maintenance Notices** – Occasionally Atlassian (the company behind Trello) posts service alerts that may affect sync.

### Step‑by‑Step Fix  

**If a simple refresh doesn’t help:**  

1. **Clear the Mobile Cache**  
   - **iOS:** Settings → Trello → *Toggle* “Clear Cache” (or uninstall and reinstall if the option isn’t present).  
   - **Android:** Settings → Apps → Trello → Storage → *Clear Cache*.  

2. **Log Out and Back In**  
   - On both desktop and mobile, sign out of Trello, close the browser or app, then sign back in. This forces a fresh authentication token and re‑pulls the board data.  

3. **Force a Full Sync**  
   - On desktop, open the board, then add a tiny, harmless edit (e.g., add a space to a card description). This triggers an immediate push to the server, prompting the mobile app to receive the update on its next sync.  

4. **Check for App Updates**  
   - An outdated mobile version can miss newer API calls. Visit the App Store or Google Play, install any pending updates, and repeat the sync steps.  

### When Sync Still Fails  

If cards still disappear after the above steps, the issue may be **board‑level permission changes** (covered later) or a **temporary server glitch**. In such cases, waiting a few minutes and trying again often resolves the problem. If the issue persists for more than an hour, contact Trello Support with the board URL and a description of the discrepancy.

---

## 2. Reclaim Missing Cards or Lists  

### Common Causes  

- **Accidental Archiving** – Cards or entire lists can be archived unintentionally.  
- **Filters** – Active filters can hide cards that meet certain criteria (e.g., label, member).  
- **Board Permissions** – A collaborator with limited rights may have moved a card to a board they can’t see.  

### Locate Archived Items  

1. **Open the Board Menu** (click the three‑dot icon on the right side).  
2. Select **“More” → “Archived Items.”**  
3. Choose **“Cards”** or **“Lists”** from the dropdown.  

You’ll see a chronological list of everything that’s been archived.  

### Restoring a Card or List  

- **Single Card**: Hover over the card entry, click **“Send to Board.”** It will reappear at the top of its original list.  
- **Whole List**: Click the **“Restore”** button next to the list name. The list returns with all its cards in the original order.  

### If the Item Isn’t Archived  

1. **Check Active Filters**  
   - Open the board menu → **“Filter Cards.”**  
   - Turn off all filter toggles. If the missing cards reappear, note which filter was hiding them and adjust accordingly.  

2. **Search the Board**  
   - Use the **search bar** (top‑right) and type a keyword from the missing card’s title. Trello’s global search can locate cards even if they’re on a hidden list.  

3. **Review Activity Log**  
   - Board menu → **“Activity.”** Scroll through recent actions to see if someone moved or renamed the card. The log shows who performed each action, helping you track down the card’s new location.  

### Prevent Future Vanishings  

- **Enable “Show Archive” shortcuts** – Add the **“Show Archived Items”** button to your board’s quick‑access bar for easy reference.  
- **Educate Team Members** – Briefly explain the difference between “archiving” and “deleting” during onboarding (refer to Chapter 6 on Collaboration).  

---

## 3. Troubleshooting Power‑Up or Automation Errors  

Power‑Ups and Butler automations extend Trello’s capabilities, but they rely on external services and scripts that can fail.  

### Typical Error Messages  

- **“Power‑Up failed to load.”**  
- **“Butler command could not be completed.”**  
- **“Rate limit exceeded.”**  

### General Debugging Flow  

1. **Identify the Scope** – Does the error affect a single board, all boards, or only a specific Power‑Up?  
2. **Check Power‑Up Status** – Some Power‑Ups require a separate subscription; verify that the account is still active.  
3. **Review Automation Logs** – Butler provides a **“Command Log”** (Board menu → **“Automation” → “Command Log”**) that shows which commands succeeded or failed.  

### Fixing Power‑Up Loading Problems  

- **Refresh the Power‑Up**  
  - Open the board menu → **“Power‑Ups”** → locate the problematic Power‑Up → click **“Refresh.”**  

- **Re‑Authorize the Integration**  
  - Some Power‑Ups (e.g., Google Drive, Slack) need OAuth tokens. Click **“Configure”** and follow the prompts to re‑grant access.  

- **Disable and Re‑Enable**  
  - Turn the Power‑Up **off**, wait a few seconds, then turn it **on** again. This resets the internal connection.  

- **Check Browser Extensions**  
  - Ad blockers or privacy extensions can block third‑party scripts. Temporarily disable them and see if the Power‑Up works.  

### Fixing Butler Automation Errors  

1. **Inspect the Command**  
   - In the **Command Log**, locate the failing command. Click the entry to view the exact rule (e.g., “when a card is moved to List ‘Done’, add the label ‘Completed’”).  

2. **Common Causes & Fixes**  

   - **Missing Card Data** – If a rule references a checklist that no longer exists, update the rule to use the current checklist name.  
   - **Rate Limits** – Butler limits the number of actions per month for free accounts. Reduce the frequency of heavy automations or upgrade the plan.  
   - **Syntax Errors** – When editing a rule manually, a stray character can break it. Use the built‑in **“Validate”** button before saving.  

3. **Test the Rule**  
   - After editing, click **“Test”** (if available) or perform a manual trigger (e.g., move a test card) to confirm the automation runs as expected.  

### When All Else Fails  

- **Export the Board** (Board menu → **“More” → “Export JSON”**) to keep a backup of your data.  
- **Contact Power‑Up Support** – Most third‑party Power‑Ups list a support email or help center link in their configuration pane.  

---

## 4. Handling Permission Problems When Inviting Collaborators  

### Understanding Trello Permissions  

- **Board Member** – Full access to edit cards, lists, and settings.  
- **Observer** – Can view but cannot edit (available on Business Class).  
- **Guest** – Limited to specific boards; cannot see other boards in the same team.  

### Symptom: New Invitee Can’t See the Board  

1. **Invitation Not Sent** – Double‑check the email address entered. Typos are common.  
2. **Pending Acceptance** – The invited user must click the link in the invitation email. Remind them to check spam folders.  

### Step‑by‑Step Permission Fix  

1. **Open the Board Menu → “Members.”**  
2. Locate the user’s name:  

   - **If the name is greyed out** – The invitation is pending. Resend the invite by clicking the three‑dot menu next to the name and selecting **“Resend Invite.”**  
   - **If the name is missing** – Add the user again, ensuring the correct email.  

3. **Adjust Role**  
   - Click the user’s current role (e.g., “Member”) → choose **“Observer”** or **“Admin”** based on the needed access level.  

4. **Check Team Visibility**  
   - If the board belongs to a **team**, verify that the team’s privacy setting (private, visible, or public) allows the new member to join. Team admins can modify this in **Team Settings**.  

### Permission Errors with Power‑Ups  

Some Power‑Ups (e.g., Google Drive) require the user to grant additional scopes. If a collaborator receives an error like **“You don’t have permission to view this attachment,”** they must:

1. Open the Power‑Up configuration (Board menu → Power‑Ups → *specific Power‑Up*).  
2. Click **“Connect”** or **“Authorize.”**  
3. Follow the OAuth flow to grant the needed permissions.  

### Preventing Future Permission Frustrations  

- **Create a “Team Invite” Checklist** – Add a checklist to a “Welcome” card that lists steps for new members (accept invite, verify email, grant Power‑Up access).  
- **Use “Admin” Role Sparingly** – Reserve full admin rights for a small core group to avoid accidental permission changes.  

---

## 5. Restoring an Accidentally Deleted Board  

### How Deletions Occur  

- **Manual Deletion** – Clicking **“Delete Board”** in the board menu.  
- **Bulk Deletion** – Some Power‑Ups or third‑party integrations can delete multiple boards (rare, but possible).  

### Immediate Recovery Options  

1. **Undo Prompt**  
   - Right after deletion, Trello shows an **“Undo”** banner at the top of the screen. Click it immediately to restore the board.  

2. **Board Archive**  
   - Deleted boards are not placed in the **Archived Items** view; they are permanently removed from the account after 30 days. However, if the board was **archived** rather than deleted, you can recover it via **Board Menu → “More” → “Archived Items.”**  

### Restoring via Trello Support  

If the “Undo” window has passed, you still have a chance:  

1. **Gather Information**  
   - Board name, URL (if you have it), date and time of deletion, and the account email that owned the board.  

2. **Submit a Support Ticket**  
   - Visit **https://trello.com/contact** → choose **“Board Deletion”** as the issue type. Provide the details collected above.  

3. **What to Expect**  
   - Trello’s support team can often restore a board within 24‑48 hours, provided the request is within 30 days of deletion.  

### Preventing Irreversible Deletions  

- **Enable “Board Deletion Confirmation”** – In **Personal Settings → “Board Settings,”** turn on the extra confirmation checkbox. This adds a second “Are you sure?” prompt.  
- **Use “Archive” Rather Than Delete** – When you think a board may be needed later, archive it. It stays hidden but can be restored anytime.  

---

## 6. A Systematic Troubleshooting Checklist  

When you encounter any Trello hiccup, run through this quick checklist before diving into deeper fixes:

| Issue | Quick Check | First Action |
|-------|-------------|--------------|
| Sync mismatch | Is internet stable? | Refresh both devices |
| Missing card/list | Is it archived? | Open **Archived Items** |
| Power‑Up error | Is the Power‑Up enabled? | Refresh or re‑authorize |
| Automation failure | See Butler **Command Log** | Validate the rule |
| Invitee can’t see board | Invitation status? | Resend or correct email |
| Deleted board | Undo banner visible? | Click **Undo** |

If the problem persists after the first action, proceed to the detailed steps in the relevant section above.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Sync problems** are usually resolved by refreshing, clearing caches, and ensuring both devices use the same account.  
- **Missing cards or lists** are often hidden in the archive or filtered view; use the board’s **Archived Items** and **Filter** tools to locate them.  
- **Power‑Ups and Butler automations** rely on external connections; re‑authorizing, refreshing, or adjusting rate limits typically restores functionality.  
- **Permission glitches** stem from pending invitations, wrong roles, or missing OAuth authorizations—verify member status and Power‑Up scopes.  
- **Accidental board deletions** can be undone immediately via the on‑screen banner; otherwise, contact Trello Support within 30 days.  
- A **standard troubleshooting checklist** helps you act quickly, minimizing downtime and keeping your workflow visible.  

Armed with these strategies, you can turn Trello’s occasional hiccups into routine maintenance—keeping your projects on track and your team focused on what matters most.
