# Chapter 9: Advanced Board Views: Calendar, Dashboard, and Timeline

## Switching Between Board, Calendar, and Timeline Views  

Imagine you’re coordinating a product launch that involves design, development, and marketing. The **Board view** gives you a classic Kanban layout—cards move from “Ideas” to “In Progress” to “Done.” But as the launch date approaches, you need to see *when* each task is due, and how the work fits together over weeks. That’s where the **Calendar** and **Timeline** views become indispensable.

### How to toggle views  

1. **Locate the view selector** – In the upper‑right corner of any board, click the **“Views”** icon (it looks like a grid).  
2. **Choose your view** – A dropdown lists the available options: **Board**, **Calendar**, and **Timeline**.  
3. **Remember your last choice** – Trello remembers the view you selected, so the next time you open the board it will open in the same mode.  

> **Tip:** You can keep the Board view open in one browser tab while exploring Calendar or Timeline in another tab. This makes side‑by‑side comparison easy for multi‑stakeholder meetings.

## Using the Calendar View Effectively  

The Calendar view turns every card’s **due date** into a visual event on a monthly grid. It’s the fastest way to answer the question, “What’s due when?”

### Setting up cards for the Calendar  

- **Add a due date** – Open a card, click the **Due Date** field, and pick a date (and optionally a time). The card instantly appears on the Calendar.  
- **Use reminders** – If you enabled reminders in earlier chapters, they still fire, but now you also see the upcoming reminder as a shaded bar on the calendar.  

### Navigating the Calendar  

| Action | How to do it |
|--------|--------------|
| **Switch months** | Click the left/right arrows at the top of the calendar, or use ⟨ ← ⟩ / ⟨ → ⟩ keyboard shortcuts. |
| **Toggle weeks** | Click the **“Week”** button to zoom in; click **“Month”** to zoom out. |
| **Drag‑and‑drop** | Grab a card on the calendar and drop it on a new date to reschedule. Trello updates the card’s due date automatically. |
| **Show/hide weekends** | Click the gear icon → **Settings** → toggle **“Show weekends”**. This cleans up the view for teams that only work weekdays. |

### Filtering within the Calendar  

1. Click the **Filter** button (the funnel icon) in the Calendar toolbar.  
2. Choose one or more of the following criteria:  

   - **Labels** – e.g., only “Marketing” cards.  
   - **Members** – e.g., tasks assigned to *Alex*.  
   - **Due date range** – e.g., “Next 14 days”.  

3. The calendar instantly redraws, showing only the matching cards.  

> **Scenario:** Your marketing lead wants to see only the campaigns scheduled for the next two weeks. They filter by the “Marketing” label and the “Next 14 days” date range, giving a clean, focused view.

## Getting Insight with the Dashboard Power‑Up  

Visual reports turn raw card data into charts you can share in meetings or embed in presentations. The **Dashboard Power‑Up** is Trello’s native analytics add‑on; it does not require a third‑party subscription.

### Enabling the Dashboard Power‑Up  

1. Open the **Power‑Ups** menu (refer to Chapter 8).  
2. Search for **“Dashboard”** and click **Add**.  
3. The Dashboard appears as a new tab on your board, alongside Board, Calendar, and Timeline.  

### Building a useful dashboard  

When you first open the Dashboard, you’ll see a set of **widgets**—small visual components you can add, move, or remove. Common widgets for a launch board include:

- **Cards by List** – a bar chart showing how many cards sit in each list (e.g., “Design”, “Development”, “QA”).  
- **Cards by Label** – a pie chart that breaks down work by label (e.g., “Feature”, “Bug”, “Marketing”).  
- **Cards by Due Date** – a line chart that visualizes upcoming workload over the next 30 days.  
- **Burn‑up Chart** – useful for Agile teams; tracks completed versus total work over time.  

To add a widget: click **“Add Widget”**, select the type, then configure the filter (e.g., only cards with the “Sprint 1” label).  

### Interpreting the dashboard  

- **High‑density bars** in “Cards by List” indicate bottlenecks—perhaps “Development” has too many cards waiting.  
- **Large slices** in “Cards by Label” reveal where effort is concentrated—maybe “Bug” takes up 40 % of the board, prompting a quality‑focus meeting.  
- **Burn‑up trends** that plateau suggest the team may need extra resources or scope adjustment.  

### Exporting and sharing  

- Click the **Export** icon on the Dashboard tab to download a CSV file of the underlying data.  
- Use the **Share** button to generate a public link (read‑only) that you can embed in Slack or email.  

## Filtering Cards Across All Views  

Filters are a universal way to narrow focus, no matter whether you’re looking at the Board, Calendar, or Timeline.

### The filter toolbar  

- **Location** – The funnel icon appears in the top‑right of each view.  
- **Options** – You can filter by **due date**, **label**, **member**, and **keyword** (searches titles and descriptions).  

### Step‑by‑step filtering  

1. Click the funnel icon.  
2. Tick the checkboxes for the labels you want (e.g., “Design”).  
3. Choose a member from the dropdown (e.g., “Maria”).  
4. Optionally set a date range (e.g., “Due in the next 7 days”).  
5. Press **Apply** – All three views instantly reflect the filtered set.  

### Saving filter presets (workaround)  

Trello does not yet support permanent filter presets, but you can **bookmark** a URL that includes filter parameters. After applying a filter, copy the URL from the address bar; reopening that link restores the same filter state.  

> **Example:** The project manager creates a bookmark called “Marketing‑Week‑View” that always shows only “Marketing” cards due this week. Team members can click the bookmark to jump straight to that filtered view.

## Customizing Views for Different Team Roles or Project Phases  

One board often serves multiple audiences—designers, developers, marketers, and executives—each of whom needs a tailored visual experience.

### Role‑based view defaults  

1. **Create a view‑specific shortcut** – In the **Views** dropdown, hover over a view (e.g., Timeline) and click the **pin** icon. This pins the view as a quick‑access button for anyone who opens the board.  
2. **Communicate defaults** – In the board description or a pinned card, note which view each role should start with (e.g., “Developers: open in Timeline”).

Imagine you’re launching a new smartphone. The effort involves three distinct teams: **Marketing**, **Engineering**, and **Customer Support**. Each team needs its own workflow—campaign planning, sprint tracking, and issue triage—yet the project’s success depends on how well these workflows stay aligned. Trying to jam all of that into a single board quickly becomes chaotic: lists overflow, cards get lost, and stakeholders can’t see the pieces that matter to them.  

Using **multiple boards** lets each team work in a space that matches its language and cadence, while **templates** and **board links** keep the whole effort synchronized. This chapter shows you how to set up that structure from scratch, reuse it for future launches, and keep your Trello workspace tidy.

---

## Building a Reusable Project Template  

A **Board Template** is a ready‑made skeleton you can copy whenever a similar project starts. Think of it as a “master copy” that contains the essential Lists, boilerplate Cards, and any Power‑Ups you want to carry over.

### 1. Sketch the Core Stages  

1. **Identify the universal phases** of the project type.  
   - For a product launch: `Planning → Design → Development → QA → Release → Post‑Launch`.  
2. **Create a List for each phase** on a new board.  
   - Because you already know how to add Lists (see Chapter 3), simply click **Add another list** and name it accordingly.  

### 2. Add Boilerplate Cards  

Boilerplate cards are the “starter tasks” that appear on every new board of this type.  

- **Example Card:** *Kick‑off meeting* (placed in the `Planning` list).  
- **Checklist:** Add a checklist named **Launch Checklist** with items like “Define target audience”, “Set launch date”, “Prepare press kit”.  

Using **Checklists**, **Due dates**, and **Labels** (introduced earlier) on these cards gives every copy a consistent baseline.

### 3. Turn the Board into a Template  

1. Open the board’s **Menu** (right‑hand side).  
2. Select **More** → **Settings** → **Convert to Template**.  
3. Confirm the conversion.  

The board now displays a **Template** badge. Whenever you need a new launch board, you’ll start from this exact layout, saving hours of setup.

---

## Duplicating a Board for a New Project  

When a fresh project kicks off—say, the next smartphone model—you don’t have to rebuild the board manually. You **duplicate** (or **copy**) the template.

### Using the “Copy Board” Feature  

1. From the **Home** view, locate the template board.  
2. Click the three‑dot **⋯** menu on the board thumbnail.  
3. Choose **Copy Board**.  
4. In the dialog, give the new board a specific name (e.g., *Galaxy X Launch – Q4 2026*).  
5. Decide whether to copy **Cards**, **Lists**, **Board Settings**, and **Power‑Ups**. For a template, you’ll usually keep everything except the **attachments** that are project‑specific.  

### What Gets Copied vs. What Stays Unique  

| Copied | Remains Unique |
|--------|----------------|
| Lists and their order | Board background & cover image (you can change later) |
| Boilerplate cards (with checklists, labels) | Card members, due dates, comments (they’re cleared on copy) |
| Enabled Power‑Ups | Board members (you’ll add the current team) |

By default, Trello strips out members, comments, and due dates, giving you a clean slate while preserving the structure you need.

---

## Connecting Boards for Cross‑Project Visibility  

Even though each team works on its own board, they often need to see each other’s progress. Trello offers two straightforward ways to link boards: **card linking** and the **Board Link Power‑Up**.

### Linking Cards Across Boards  

1. Open a card on the **Marketing** board that represents the “Launch Campaign”.  
2. In the **Add to card** field, type `@` followed by the name of the board you want to reference (e.g., `@Engineering`).  
3. Select the target board, then choose the specific card (e.g., “Beta Firmware Ready”).  

The original card now shows a **linked card** section at the bottom, providing a clickable shortcut to the related item on the other board. This method works without any additional Power‑Ups.

### Using the Board Link Power‑Up  

If you prefer a visual pane that lists related boards:

1. Open the board’s **Menu** → **Power‑Ups**.  
2. Search for **Board Links** (a native Power‑Up) and click **Add**.  
3. Click **Add Link** on the board, give it a label like “Engineering Board”, and select the board to connect.  

The linked board appears as a card on the current board, making it easy for anyone to hop between contexts.

### Example: Marketing ↔ Design ↔ Support  

- **Marketing Card:** “Press Release Draft” links to the **Design** board’s card “Product Images”.  
- **Support Card:** “FAQ Draft” links to the **Marketing** board’s card “Launch Date Announcement”.  

Whenever a linked card is moved to a new List, the reference updates automatically, keeping every stakeholder in the loop.

---

## Navigating Quickly with the Home Dashboard  

When you manage dozens of boards, finding the right one at a glance is crucial. Trello’s **Home** view is the central hub for board navigation.

### The Home Layout  

- **Recent Boards** – shows the boards you’ve visited in the last 30 days.  
- **Starred Boards** – boards you’ve **starred** for fast access (click the star icon on any board).  
- **Team Sections** – groups boards by the team you belong to.  

Because you already know how to **star** a board (click the star next to its name), you can create a personal “quick‑launch” area for all your active project boards.

### Pinning Favorite Boards  

1. Open the board you use most (e.g., *Current Sprint*).  
2. Click the star icon at the top of the board.  
3. The board now appears at the top of the **Starred Boards** list on Home.  

You can star as many boards as you like; Home will automatically sort them by most‑recent activity.

### Using Filters and Search  

- **Search bar** (top‑right) lets you type a board name, label, or card title.  
- **Filters** (click the funnel icon) let you narrow results by **Team**, **Board Visibility** (private, team‑visible, public), or **Labels**.  

These tools become indispensable when you have multiple launch boards across several product lines.

---

## Keeping the Workspace Clean: Archiving Completed Boards  

A cluttered board list makes it harder to locate active projects. Trello distinguishes between **archiving** (soft delete) and **deleting** (permanent removal). For most workflows, you’ll **archive** completed boards.

### Archive vs. Delete  

- **Archive** – moves the board to the **Archived Boards** section; you can restore it later.  
- **Delete** – permanently erases the board and all its data; recovery is impossible.  

Because you may need to reference a past launch for reporting, archiving is the safer default.

### Bulk Archiving Steps  

1. From **Home**, click **Boards** → **View All Boards**.  
2. Click the **Filter** icon and select **Closed Boards** to see already archived items.  
3. To archive a board: open the board, go to **Menu** → **More** → **Close Board**.  
4. Confirm the action. The board disappears from your active list and appears under **Closed Boards**.  

If you have many finished boards, repeat the process or use a **Butler** rule (covered in Chapter 7) to automatically close a board when its last card is moved to a “Done” list.

### Restoring an Archived Board  

1. In **Home**, click **Boards** → **Closed Boards**.  
2. Locate the board you want to bring back.  
3. Click **Reopen**.  

The board returns to its original position, preserving all Lists and Cards exactly as they were when closed.

---

## Tips for Scaling Multi‑Board Workflows  

Even with templates and links, large programs can become unwieldy. The following habits make the system sustainable.

- **Naming Conventions** – start every board with a consistent prefix, e.g., `Launch – <Product> – <Quarter>`. This makes searching and sorting easier.  
- **Cross‑Board Labels** – create a set of standard Labels (e.g., **Urgent**, **Blocked**, **Milestone**) and apply them across all boards. When you filter by a label on Home, you’ll see every card sharing that status, regardless of board.  
- **Butler Automation** – set up a simple rule: *When a board is copied from a template, add the “New Project” label to all cards in the first list.* This keeps the new board’s tasks highlighted without manual effort.  
- **Regular Clean‑Up Cadence** – schedule a monthly review to archive boards that have been closed for more than 30 days.  

By embedding these practices early, you’ll avoid the “board sprawl” that plagues many growing teams.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Board Templates** let you capture a repeatable project skeleton—including Lists, boilerplate Cards, and Power‑Ups—so you can spin up new projects in minutes.  
- **Copying a board** from a template preserves structure while clearing out members, comments, and due dates, giving you a clean starting point.  
- **Linking cards** or using the **Board Links Power‑Up** creates live connections between related boards, enabling cross‑team visibility without duplicating information.  
- The **Home dashboard** centralizes navigation; starring, filtering, and searching let you jump to any active board instantly.  
- **Archiving** finished boards (instead of deleting) keeps your workspace tidy while preserving history for future reference; you can restore them anytime.  

With these tools, you can confidently scale Trello from single‑board tasks to full‑fledged, multi‑board projects—maintaining clarity, speed, and control every step of the way.

# Chapter 12: Best Practices for Trello Organization: Tips from the Pros

## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Imagine Maya, a freelance graphic designer who juggles client work, personal projects, and a side hustle selling prints online. She started with a single Trello **Board** for each client, but over months the boards multiplied: “Client A – Design,” “Client A – Feedback,” “Print Shop,” “Ideas,” “Marketing,” and a catch‑all “Stuff To Do.” When Maya opens Trello, she sees a sprawling list of boards, each brimming with cards, labels, and a handful of **Power‑Ups** she tried once and forgot about. She spends more time searching for the right board than actually designing.

Maya’s story is common. The good news? A handful of proven habits—what the pros call “clean board” strategies—can turn that chaos into a clear, focused workspace. The following sections walk you through each habit, showing how to apply it step‑by‑step, even if you’re just starting out.

---

## 1. Embrace the “One Board, One Purpose” Rule  

### Why a Single Purpose Matters  

A **Board** is a digital canvas that makes work visible. When a board tries to serve several unrelated purposes, the visual hierarchy collapses: cards from different projects compete for attention, filters become noisy, and the board’s original intent gets lost. Keeping each board dedicated to a single purpose restores the clarity that makes Kanban so powerful.

### How to Identify a Board’s Core Purpose  

1. **Write a one‑sentence mission** for the board.  
   *Example:* “Track all tasks for the ‘Spring Launch’ marketing campaign.”  
2. **List the types of work** the board should contain. If anything falls outside that list, it belongs elsewhere.  
3. **Ask yourself:** “If I had to delete this board tomorrow, what would I lose?” If the answer is vague, the board is probably too broad.

### Auditing Your Existing Boards  

1. **Gather all boards** on the Trello home screen.  
2. **For each board**, read its mission statement (add one if missing).  
3. **Group boards** that share the same purpose.  
4. **Consolidate or split**:  
   * If two boards serve the same purpose, merge them.  
   * If one board covers multiple purposes, create separate boards and move the relevant cards.  

### Quick Checklist  

- ✅ Each board has a clear, written purpose.  
- ✅ No board mixes unrelated projects or workflows.  
- ✅ Boards are named to reflect their purpose (e.g., “Blog Content Calendar”).  

---

## 2. Use Labels Consistently for Instant Visual Filtering  

### The Power of a Well‑Defined Label System  

Labels are the colored tags you already know from earlier chapters. When used consistently, they become a glance‑readable map of priority, department, or status—no need to open each card.

### Building a Simple Label Scheme  

| Color | Suggested Use | Example Name |
|-------|---------------|--------------|
| Red   | **Urgent / High Priority** | “Urgent” |
| Orange| **Waiting / Blocked** | “On Hold” |
| Yellow| **Ideas / To Explore** | “Idea” |
| Green | **Completed / Done** | “Done” |
| Blue  | **Team / Department** | “Design” |
| Purple| **Client / Category** | “Client A” |

**Tip:** Start with **three** core colors (e.g., priority, status, team) and expand only when you truly need more distinction.

### Applying Labels Without Overwhelm  

1. **Create a label cheat‑sheet** in the board description or a dedicated “Reference” card.  
2. **Assign labels at card creation** (you can set default labels in the board settings).  
3. **Use the filter bar** (top right) to toggle one or more labels and instantly view a focused slice of work.  

### Consistency Checklist  

- ✅ Labels are limited to a manageable set (no more than 6–8 per board).  
- ✅ Each label has a clear, documented meaning.  
- ✅ Team members understand and use the same label conventions.  

---

## 3. Keep Active Lists to 5‑7 for Maximum Focus  

### Why Fewer Lists Work Better  

Lists represent workflow stages or time‑based categories. When you exceed 7 active lists, the board’s vertical space becomes crowded, and it’s harder to spot bottlenecks. A lean list structure also aligns with the classic Kanban principle of limiting work‑in‑progress (WIP).

### Designing a Streamlined List Layout  

A typical “one‑purpose” board might follow this pattern:

1. **Backlog** – ideas not yet scheduled  
2. **To Do** – tasks ready to start  
3. **In Progress** – work currently underway  
4. **Review** – awaiting feedback or approval  
5. **Done** – completed items  

If you need extra granularity (e.g., “Waiting for Client”), consider **sub‑lists** via **Checklists** inside a card, or use **labels** instead of an additional list.

### Managing Overflow  

- **Archive finished lists**: Click the list’s menu → “Archive List.”  
- **Create a “Future” list** for items that will become active later; keep it minimal.  
- **Use the “Search” function** to locate cards that belong elsewhere rather than adding a new list.  

### List‑Limit Checklist  

- ✅ No more than 7 active lists are visible at any time.  
- ✅ Each list has a clear purpose that aligns with the board’s mission.  
- ✅ Overflow or completed lists are archived regularly.  

---

## 4. Schedule Regular Board Cleanups  

### The 15‑Minute Weekly Reset  

A board that is tidy today can become messy tomorrow. Setting a recurring **weekly cleanup** habit (e.g., every Friday at 4 pm) prevents clutter from snowballing.

### Weekly Cleanup Routine  

1. **Review “To Do” and “In Progress”**: Move any stale cards to the appropriate list or archive them if they’re no longer relevant.  
2. **Archive completed cards**: Use the board menu → “Archive All Cards” in the “Done” list.  
3. **Check labels**: Remove any that are no longer used; update the cheat‑sheet.  
4. **Evaluate Power‑Ups**: Disable any you haven’t used in the past month.  
5. **Rename or reorder lists** if the workflow has changed.  

### Automating the Cleanup (Optional)  

If you’re comfortable with **Butler**, you can create a rule such as:  
> “Every Sunday at 6 am, move cards in ‘Done’ that are older than 7 days to the archive.”

Even a simple manual routine, however, yields huge productivity gains.

### Cleanup Checklist  

- ✅ Stale cards have been moved or archived.  
- ✅ Unused labels are removed.  
- ✅ Power‑Ups are reviewed and trimmed.  
- ✅ Lists reflect the current workflow.  

---

## 5. Avoid Over‑Customizing with Too Many Power‑Ups  

### The Temptation of “Shiny New Features”  

Power‑Ups extend Trello with third‑party integrations (e.g., Calendar, Google Drive). While they can be game‑changing, each added Power‑Up consumes system resources and adds visual noise. The pros recommend **capping Power‑Ups at three per board**—enough to get the most value without overwhelming the interface.

### Choosing the Right Power‑Ups  

1. **Identify a concrete need** (e.g., “I need to see due dates on a calendar”).  
2. **Search the Power‑Ups directory** for the simplest tool that meets that need.  
3. **Enable it** and test for a week. If it doesn’t become part of your workflow, disable it.  

### Commonly Recommended Power‑Ups  

| Need | Recommended Power‑Up |
|------|----------------------|
| Calendar view of due dates | **Calendar** |
| Visualizing metrics | **Dashboard** |
| Connecting to a file repository | **Google Drive** (or **OneDrive**) |
| Automating repetitive actions | **Butler** (already covered) |

### Managing Power‑Ups  

- **Turn off unused Power‑Ups**: Board menu → “Power‑Ups” → “Disable.”  
- **Document active Power‑Ups** in a “Board Settings” card for team reference.  

### Power‑Up Checklist  

- ✅ No more than three Power‑Ups are active on any board.  
- ✅ Each Power‑Up solves a specific, recurring need.  
- ✅ Unused Power‑Ups are disabled and documented.  

---

## 6. Putting It All Together: A Sample Clean Board  

Below is a snapshot of a board that follows every best practice discussed. Feel free to replicate the structure in your own Trello workspace.

| **Board Name** | **Purpose** |
|----------------|------------|
| “Spring Launch – Marketing” | Track all tasks needed to launch the spring product line. |

### Lists (5 Active)  

1. **Backlog** – ideas and postponed tasks.  
2. **To Do** – tasks ready to start this week.  
3. **In Progress** – work currently being done.  
4. **Review** – awaiting stakeholder feedback.  
5. **Done** – completed tasks (archived weekly).  

### Labels (6 Consistent Colors)  

- **Red – Urgent**

## 1. Sync Issues Between Desktop and Mobile Apps  

### Why Sync Can Fail  
Even though Trello stores everything in the cloud, the desktop web client and the mobile app maintain **local caches** to speed up loading. If the cache becomes outdated or the device loses internet connectivity, the two views can drift apart.

### Quick Diagnostic Checklist  

1. **Check Internet Connection** – Verify that both devices are online. A weak Wi‑Fi signal or cellular dropout often causes partial sync.  
2. **Refresh the Board** –  
   * Desktop: Click the **Refresh** button (or press `F5`).  
   * Mobile: Pull down from the top of the board view to trigger a manual sync.  
3. **Confirm Account Consistency** – Ensure you’re signed into the same Trello account on both devices.  
4. **Look for Maintenance Notices** – Occasionally Atlassian (the company behind Trello) posts service alerts that may affect sync.

### Step‑by‑Step Fix  

**If a simple refresh doesn’t help:**  

1. **Clear the Mobile Cache**  
   - **iOS:** Settings → Trello → *Toggle* “Clear Cache” (or uninstall and reinstall if the option isn’t present).  
   - **Android:** Settings → Apps → Trello → Storage → *Clear Cache*.  

2. **Log Out and Back In**  
   - On both desktop and mobile, sign out of Trello, close the browser or app, then sign back in. This forces a fresh authentication token and re‑pulls the board data.  

3. **Force a Full Sync**  
   - On desktop, open the board, then add a tiny, harmless edit (e.g., add a space to a card description). This triggers an immediate push to the server, prompting the mobile app to receive the update on its next sync.  

4. **Check for App Updates**  
   - An outdated mobile version can miss newer API calls. Visit the App Store or Google Play, install any pending updates, and repeat the sync steps.  

### When Sync Still Fails  

If cards still disappear after the above steps, the issue may be **board‑level permission changes** (covered later) or a **temporary server glitch**. In such cases, waiting a few minutes and trying again often resolves the problem. If the issue persists for more than an hour, contact Trello Support with the board URL and a description of the discrepancy.

## 2. Reclaim Missing Cards or Lists  

### Common Causes  

- **Accidental Archiving** – Cards or entire lists can be archived unintentionally.  
- **Filters** – Active filters can hide cards that meet certain criteria (e.g., label, member).  
- **Board Permissions** – A collaborator with limited rights may have moved a card to a board they can’t see.  

### Locate Archived Items  

1. **Open the Board Menu** (click the three‑dot icon on the right side).  
2. Select **“More” → “Archived Items.”**  
3. Choose **“Cards”** or **“Lists”** from the dropdown.  

You’ll see a chronological list of everything that’s been archived.  

### Restoring a Card or List  

- **Single Card**: Hover over the card entry, click **“Send to Board.”** It will reappear at the top of its original list.  
- **Whole List**: Click the **“Restore”** button next to the list name. The list returns with all its cards in the original order.  

### If the Item Isn’t Archived  

1. **Check Active Filters**  
   - Open the board menu → **“Filter Cards.”**  
   - Turn off all filter toggles. If the missing cards reappear, note which filter was hiding them and adjust accordingly.  

2. **Search the Board**  
   - Use the **search bar** (top‑right) and type a keyword from the missing card’s title. Trello’s global search can locate cards even if they’re on a hidden list.  

3. **Review Activity Log**  
   - Board menu → **“Activity.”** Scroll through recent actions to see if someone moved or renamed the card. The log shows who performed each action, helping you track down the card’s new location.  

### Prevent Future Vanishings  

- **Enable “Show Archive” shortcuts** – Add the **“Show Archived Items”** button to your board’s quick‑access bar for easy reference.  
- **Educate Team Members** – Briefly explain the difference between “archiving” and “deleting” during onboarding (refer to Chapter 6 on Collaboration).

## 3. Troubleshooting Power‑Up or Automation Errors  

Power‑Ups and Butler automations extend Trello’s capabilities, but they rely on external services and scripts that can fail.  

### Typical Error Messages  

- **“Power‑Up failed to load.”**  
- **“Butler command could not be completed.”**  
- **“Rate limit exceeded.”**  

### General Debugging Flow  

1. **Identify the Scope** – Does the error affect a single board, all boards, or only a specific Power‑Up?  
2. **Check Power‑Up Status** – Some Power‑Ups require a separate subscription; verify that the account is still active.  
3. **Review Automation Logs** – Butler provides a **“Command Log”** (Board menu → **“Automation” → “Command Log”**) that shows which commands succeeded or failed.  

### Fixing Power‑Up Loading Problems  

- **Refresh the Power‑Up**  
  - Open the board menu → **“Power‑Ups”** → locate the problematic Power‑Up → click **“Refresh.”**  

- **Re‑Authorize the Integration**  
  - Some Power‑Ups (e.g., Google Drive, Slack) need OAuth tokens. Click **“Configure”** and follow the prompts to re‑grant access.  

- **Disable and Re‑Enable**  
  - Turn the Power‑Up **off**, wait a few seconds, then turn it **on** again. This resets the internal connection.  

- **Check Browser Extensions**  
  - Ad blockers or privacy extensions can block third‑party scripts. Temporarily disable them and see if the Power‑Up works.  

### Fixing Butler Automation Errors  

1. **Inspect the Command**  
   - In the **Command Log**, locate the failing command. Click the entry to view the exact rule (e.g., “when a card is moved to List ‘Done’, add the label ‘Completed’”).  

2. **Common Causes & Fixes**  

   - **Missing Card Data** – If a rule references a checklist that no longer exists, update the rule to use the current checklist name.  
   - **Rate Limits** – Butler limits the number of actions per month for free accounts. Reduce the frequency of heavy automations or upgrade the plan.  
   - **Syntax Errors** – When editing a rule manually, a stray character can break it. Use the built‑in **“Validate”** button before saving.  

3. **Test the Rule**  
   - After editing, click **“Test”** (if available) or perform a manual trigger (e.g., move a test card) to confirm the automation runs as expected.  

### When All Else Fails  

- **Export the Board** (Board menu → **“More” → “Export JSON”**) to keep a backup of your data.  
- **Contact Power‑Up Support** – Most third‑party Power‑Ups list a support email or help center link in their configuration pane.

## 4. Handling Permission Problems When Inviting Collaborators  

### Understanding Trello Permissions  

- **Board Member** – Full access to edit cards, lists, and settings.  
- **Observer** – Can view but cannot edit (available on Business Class).  
- **Guest** – Limited to specific boards; cannot see other boards in the same team.  

### Symptom: New Invitee Can’t See the Board  

1. **Invitation Not Sent** – Double‑check the email address entered. Typos are common.  
2. **Pending Acceptance** – The invited user must click the link in the invitation email. Remind them to check spam folders.  

### Step‑by‑Step Permission Fix  

1. **Open the Board Menu → “Members.”**  
2. Locate the user’s name:  

   - **If the name is greyed out** – The invitation is pending. Resend the invite by clicking the three‑dot menu next to the name and selecting **“Resend Invite.”**  
   - **If the name is missing** – Add the user again, ensuring the correct email.  

3. **Adjust Role**  
   - Click the user’s current role (e.g., “Member”) → choose **“Observer”** or **“Admin”** based on the needed access level.  

4. **Check Team Visibility**  
   - If the board belongs to a **team**, verify that the team’s privacy setting (private, visible, or public) allows the new member to join. Team admins can modify this in **Team Settings**.  

### Permission Errors with Power‑Ups  

Some Power‑Ups (e.g., Google Drive) require the user to grant additional scopes. If a collaborator receives an error like **“You don’t have permission to view this attachment,”** they must:

1. Open the Power‑Up configuration (Board menu → Power‑Ups → *specific Power‑Up*).  
2. Click **“Connect”** or **“Authorize.”**  
3. Follow the OAuth flow to grant the needed permissions.  

### Preventing Future Permission Frustrations  

- **Create a “Team Invite” Checklist** – Add a checklist to a “Welcome” card that lists steps for new members (accept invite, verify email, grant Power‑Up access).  
- **Use “Admin” Role Sparingly** – Reserve full admin rights for a small core group to avoid accidental permission changes.

## 5. Restoring an Accidentally Deleted Board  

### How Deletions Occur  

- **Manual Deletion** – Clicking **“Delete Board”** in the board menu.  
- **Bulk Deletion** – Some Power‑Ups or third‑party integrations can delete multiple boards (rare, but possible).  

### Immediate Recovery Options  

1. **Undo Prompt**  
   - Right after deletion, Trello shows an **“Undo”** banner at the top of the screen. Click it immediately to restore the board.  

2. **Board Archive**  
   - Deleted boards are not placed in the **Archived Items** view; they are permanently removed from the account after 30 days. However, if the board was **archived** rather than deleted, you can recover it via **Board Menu → “More” → “Archived Items.”**  

### Restoring via Trello Support  

If the “Undo” window has passed, you still have a chance:  

1. **Gather Information**  
   - Board name, URL (if you have it), date and time of deletion, and the account email that owned the board.  

2. **Submit a Support Ticket**  
   - Visit **https://trello.com/contact** → choose **“Board Deletion”** as the issue type. Provide the details collected above.  

3. **What to Expect**  
   - Trello’s support team can often restore a board within 24‑48 hours, provided the request is within 30 days of deletion.  

### Preventing Irreversible Deletions  

- **Enable “Board Deletion Confirmation”** – In **Personal Settings → “Board Settings,”** turn on the extra confirmation checkbox. This adds a second “Are you sure?” prompt.  
- **Use “Archive” Rather Than Delete** – When you think a board may be needed later, archive it. It stays hidden but can be restored anytime.

## Glossary

Here’s a **glossary of key Trello terms** with clear definitions to help you master Trello for organization, project management, and productivity:

---

### **Trello Glossary**

1. **Board**
   A visual workspace in Trello that represents a project, team, or goal. Boards contain lists, cards, and can be shared with collaborators.

2. **List**
   A column within a board that organizes tasks or stages of a workflow (e.g., "To Do," "In Progress," "Done"). Lists can be customized with labels or automations.

3. **Card**
   A single task, idea, or item within a list. Cards can include descriptions, checklists, attachments, due dates, and assignees.

4. **Checklist**
   A sub-task breakdown within a card (e.g., "Buy groceries → Milk, Eggs, Bread"). Checklists track progress toward completion.

5. **Label**
   Color-coded tags (e.g., "Urgent," "High Priority," "Work") applied to cards for quick visual categorization and filtering.

6. **Member**
   A user who has access to a board (e.g., collaborators, team members). Members can be assigned to cards or given permissions (view, edit, admin).

7. **Power-Up**
   Add-ons or integrations that extend Trello’s functionality (e.g., **Calendar View**, **Slack**, **Google Drive**, **Automation**). Some are built-in; others require enabling.

8. **Automation (Butler)**
   Trello’s built-in automation tool (named "Butler") that lets you create rules to automate repetitive tasks (e.g., moving cards when due dates pass).

9. **Due Date**
   A deadline set for a card to ensure timely completion. Overdue cards are visually marked in the calendar view or list.

10. **Attachment**
    Files (e.g., PDFs, images, documents) or links (e.g., Google Docs, Dropbox) added to a card for reference. Drag-and-drop supported.

11. **Comment**
    Notes or discussions added to a card by team members. Comments can include @mentions (e.g., "@Alex, please review") and emojis.

12. **Archived Card/List**
    Cards or lists that are hidden but not deleted. Archived items can be restored if needed. *Deleting* removes them permanently.

13. **Template**
    Pre-built boards for common use cases (e.g., **Project Management**, **Content Calendar**, **Meeting Notes**). Templates save time by providing a starting structure.

14. **Team**
    A group of boards and members organized under one workspace (e.g., "Marketing Team," "Personal Projects"). Teams simplify permissions and collaboration.

15. **Dashboard (Trello Home)**
    The main landing page showing all boards, recent activity, and quick-access tools. Useful for getting an overview of multiple projects.
